Course Overview
Welcome! You’re probably here because you are taking the course Cultural Analytics, at Leiden University. It’s part of the minor Digital Humanities and Cultural Analytics.
The course instructor is Dr. Yann Ryan.
This e-book will serve as the course website. The menu on the left side lists the chapters, grouped into one section for each class - two per week. Each section ends with any home exercises to do before the next class. At the bottom of the menu you’ll find useful information, including suggested datasets for your reports, and how to prepare for the exam. The menu on the right contains the table of contents for this particular chapter, so you can skip to different sections. There’s a search function just below the title on the left, which students have found very useful when they want to find some code we’ve discussed and use it later on in an assignment.
You’ll also need to familiarise yourself with the course Brightspace area, where I’ll put further information and you’ll submit assignments.

title: Cultural Analytics: Course Book
text:
What is Cultural Analytics?
Cultural analytics is the use of digital, computational techniques to find, analyse, and understand cultural material - the kinds of data produced by or about culture, and the people who make and consume it.
That covers a lot of ground. Cultural data comes in many forms: the text of novels, digitised newspapers, images and film, audio, and - the focus of this course - structured, tabular data: the kind of data you’d find in a spreadsheet, with rows and columns. Think of a museum’s collection database, a streaming platform’s play-count records, a historical census, or a table of shipping records. If you’re also taking a course on computational text or image analysis, that’s cultural analytics too - just applied to unstructured material rather than tables. This course is deliberately narrower and more hands-on: everything we do here starts from data you could open in a spreadsheet.
Within that scope, this course is centred on one core technique: data visualisation - the graphical representation of information and data. It’s one of the most direct ways to explore, analyse, and communicate what a structured dataset can tell us, and it’s been part of how people make sense of information since at least the eighteenth century (with maps going back much further still). Today we come across data visualisations everywhere: in scientific articles, news media, advertisements, and increasingly in the humanities and cultural sector - museums visualising their collections, cultural institutions mapping historical migration, streaming platforms illustrating listening habits.
In the humanities, the structured data we use might be, for example, historical statistics or networks, or metadata about text, images, or objects (rather than the text or images themselves). It might be something totally different such as streaming or listening data, or geographic and spatial data.

title: Cultural Analytics: Course Book
text:
Course Aims and Objectives

At the end of this course, you will:

Be able to construct data visualisations from scratch using the coding language R.
Use online publication formats such as Markdown to make professional-standard visual essays containing code, visualisations, and explanatory text.
Understand how a FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) approach to data is important for your work and that of others.
Be able to critically reflect on a range of visualisations, with a specific focus on network and spatial data.
Know where to find some of the inspiring visualisations, thinkers, and designers in this field.
Be able to discuss your views on information visualisation with peers as well as give and receive feedback.


In terms of concrete skills, by the end of this course, you should be able to use humanities-focused data to make informative, highly-customised visualisations such as this:


Show the code
library(tidyverse)
library(ggthemes)

# Summarised from the MoMA collection data: https://github.com/MuseumofModernArt/collection
df = read_csv('moma_acquisitions_gender.csv')

df = df %>% 
  filter(works >= 50) %>% 
  mutate(share_women = works_by_women / works * 100)

p1 = ggplot() + 
  geom_point(data = df, aes(year, share_women), size = 1, alpha = .5) +
  geom_smooth(data = df, aes(year, share_women), method = "loess", span = .5,
              se = FALSE, color = 'black', alpha = .75) + 
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 60)) + 
  labs(title = 'Who Gets Collected? Women Artists at MoMA', 
       subtitle = "Share of works acquired each year which were made by women, 1930 to 2025", 
       x = NULL, 
       y = "Works by women (% of acquisitions)")  +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1985, color = 'red', alpha = .6, linewidth = 2) +
  annotate("text", x = 1982, y = 45, label = "Guerrilla Girls protest", angle = 90) + 
  theme_economist()

p1









or this:


Show the code
library(ggrepel)

# Post45 Data Collective, via TidyTuesday: https://data.post45.org/
df2 = read_csv("nyt_bestsellers.csv")

df2 = df2 %>% 
  group_by(author) %>% 
  summarise(first_year = min(year), 
            titles = n(), 
            weeks = sum(total_weeks)) %>% 
  filter(weeks >= 100) %>% 
  mutate(output = case_when(titles <= 2 ~ "1 or 2", 
                            titles < 10 ~ "3 to 9", 
                            TRUE ~ "10 or more"),
         output = fct_relevel(output, "1 or 2", "3 to 9"))

top_data = df2 %>% 
  group_by(output) %>% 
  slice_max(order_by = weeks, n = 3)

p =  ggplot() + 
  geom_point(data = df2, aes(x = first_year, 
                             y = weeks, 
                             size = weeks, 
                             fill = output), 
             pch = 21, color = 'black', alpha = .6, stroke = .5) + 
  geom_label_repel(data = top_data, aes(x = first_year, 
                                        y = weeks, 
                                        label = author, 
                                        fill = output), 
                   alpha = .6, show.legend = FALSE) + 
  scale_size_area(max_size = 6) + 
  labs(title = "Two Ways to Top the Bestseller List", 
       subtitle = "Authors with 100+ weeks on the NYT fiction bestseller list, 1931-2020.\nThe top three wrote dozens of hits; Harper Lee needed only two.") + 
  theme_fivethirtyeight() + 
  labs(y = "Total weeks on the bestseller list", 
       size = "Weeks on list: ", fill = 'Number of bestsellers: ') + 
  theme(legend.position = 'bottom', 
        legend.box = "vertical", 
        legend.margin = margin())

p









Perhaps most importantly, you will have total control over every aspect of the visualisation, from the colours, to the titles, labels, and scales. Use the ‘show the code’ button above the visualisation to see the code it was made from.
Your most important pieces of work will be two Markdown reports: publishable documents containing code, text, and data visualisations, which show off the skills you have learned during the course.

Data, Visualised…
Most importantly, you’ll learn the basic principles of data visualisation, and put them into practice using a platform called R (more on that below). R is widely used by, for example, data journalists at the BBC, and in publications like The Economist and the Financial Times.
Using a language like R or python instead of Excel or a simple application for visualising data has many advantages. For one, it’s much easier to work with large datasets. You want to analyse a museum’s entire collection, like the 160,000 works behind the first chart above, or huge datasets of movies like these ones, with millions of rows of data? It’ll take a split second in R. A second advantage is that everything you make can be reproducible, meaning your visualisations and analyses can be scientifically checked and verified.
The visualisations above were made with a few lines of the R language. If you click the ‘Show the code’ button above them, you’ll see the code I used to create them. It might look a little complicated now, but if you follow the course, you should be able to make similar (and hopefully much nicer) ones by the end of the seven-week block.
In your assignments, you’ll combine text, data and visual outputs to make a report on a topic you’re interested in. You’ll make a document like this. For this course, it’s more than enough to stick to the basic charts like the above. But if you’re interested, you can explore fancier things such as interactive maps and charts, 3D-rendered visualisations, and more.


…and the Humanities
This is not to say the course will be an exhaustive ‘how to’ for scientific data visualisations. One of your superpowers as a humanities student is that you learn to move beyond the surface level and consider the subtexts, biases, and so forth in cultural objects. In this course, we’ll put those skills to good use, and you’ll use your own expertise and interests to tell compelling and truthful stories about humanities subjects, using data.
Just as importantly, you’ll learn how to critique data visualisations and design. As a group we’ll ask: what makes them good or bad, scientific or unethical? Can we trust the intentions behind commercial or political data visualisations? Can we spot when they are being misleading, and describe exactly how? What are the negative and positive connotations around certain graphical representations, and why do we use them? How can we make better, more ethical data visualisations? How can we make visualisations which properly consider those with accessibility needs?

title: Cultural Analytics: Course Book
text:
Data Visualisation
Data visualisation is the main technique we’ll use to work with structured cultural data on this course. In practice, creating data visualisations involves mapping numerical data of some sort to graphical representations - often called geometries. A geometry might be the length of a line, the x and y position on a graph, or the temperature of a colour on a map. A good data visualisation will use this mapping to tell a story about the data, while representing it faithfully.

What will I actually do on this course?
You’ll put these skills into practice using a tool called R. R is a coding language often used for data science - it’s particularly good at working with what are called ‘dataframes’: structured data in the form of rows and columns which we’ll mostly be using on this course.
To begin with, you’ll practise the basics using interactive code snippets embedded directly in this book. Later, you’ll work in RStudio on your own computer, where you can import data, export visualisations, and code in a ‘real world’ way.
Using a coding language like this allows us to have direct control over every aspect of a visualisation - we can choose from many different geometries depending on our data and what we want to show, adjust the colours in precise ways, and pick the scale we want to use. We can also use R to summarise data, or limit it to just the parts we want to work with. This will complement the learning of Python you’re doing in your other course.
In this course, you’ll learn these very practical skills. It might be hard-going or frustrating at first, but it is very worthwhile. Skills in R or any other programming language are very valuable to all sorts of employers.
At the same time, there is one important thing to note:
Your grade for any assessment will never be dependent on your coding ability.
This is not a coding course: some of you may pick it up straight away, and others may stay at a basic level throughout the course. That is completely fine. You are welcome to ask for help from me, your peers, and online. In all your assessments, I’ll take into account your understanding of data science and visualisations on a more fundamental, humanities-led level.
It’s easy to get stuck or lost in assignments. When you’re learning a new skill like coding, you can spend many hours agonising over what might turn out to be a simple problem when it’s explained to you.
The key is to stick strictly to the number of hours given to each assignment - don’t waste lots of time working out what might turn out to be a small mistake. Set a timer and stop when it runs out - make a note and we can discuss what went wrong in the next class.

Assessment

Reports
The main assignments on this course are two reports: short visual essays, written in R Markdown, which use a dataset to explore a question you’re interested in. Each report combines explanatory text, code, and visualisations - like the examples on the data page, on a smaller scale.

Report 1: data visualisation (due Monday 23 November). Around 1,200-1,500 words, with three or four visualisations made with ggplot2.
Report 2: map (due Monday 14 December). Around 1,200-1,500 words, with at least two maps, plus other visualisations if you wish. You can use the same dataset as Report 1, or a new one.

In both reports, you should explain your question, where your data comes from and how it was made, what you did to it, and what your visualisations show - and reflect on the limitations of the data and your choices. See the data page for suggested datasets. Submit both the .Rmd file and the knitted html as a .zip file on Brightspace.


Home exercises and checkpoints
Each week has home exercises. Most are ungraded practice, but they’re the best way to prepare for the reports and the exam, so do them all. Two of them are checkpoints, which are submitted on Brightspace and graded pass/fail, to make sure everyone is comfortable with the basics of data analysis before starting Report 1:

Home exercise 2 (due Tuesday 3 November)
Home exercise 4 (due Tuesday 10 November)

You pass a checkpoint by making a genuine attempt at all of the exercises - they don’t have to be perfect.


Exam
The exam (Tuesday 5 January 2027, two hours) tests your understanding of the ideas behind the course: reading and reasoning about code, critiquing visualisations, and planning an analysis. You won’t need to use R. See Preparing for the Exam for full details and a practice exam.

The Fine Print
Attendance is required. If you know you will need to miss a class, please indicate this at least two weeks prior. If you know beforehand you will have to miss three or more classes, you cannot take this course. If you miss a class due to sickness or other unforeseen circumstances, please notify me without delay.
Class participation is part of your final grade. Aside from participation being part of your grade, I really appreciate your input. If you think you have something to ask, please speak up: there are no stupid questions, but there are a lot of lost opportunities for information exchange and learning. This field is full of exciting new ideas and developments and it is impossible to be aware of them all. So, if you can share information on an idea, article, project, or tool that is of you value to you, please do!
If you need to speak to me, I’m happy to arrange a meeting to discuss any issues or problems you encounter on the course. Ideally, send a request a week in advance, via email.
Plagiarism: If you have not done so already, please inform yourself on Leiden University’s views and regulations on plagiarism. This Leiden university library portal has several accessible web courses on how to quote and cite right and tips for bibliographic management. Note that plagiarism, copyright and other information sharing or copying issues are often extra complex when dealing with digital sources. If you are still in doubt whether (parts of) any work for this course may constitute plagiarism, you need to signal and verify this with me before you hand it in for grading.

Use of Chatbots for assignments
Generative language models or chatbots are clearly very useful tools and could probably provide code for most of this course with ease. You will likely use them throughout your studies and career. However, they are of little use if you don’t understand the absolute fundamentals of programming and computational thinking, which this course aims to teach.
Therefore, the use of chatbots for assignments on this course is specifically forbidden. It is much better to attempt and fail rather than submit something created by a chatbot which you don’t understand. Throughout the course, I will ask you to explain your submitted code line by line. If it looks likely to have been created by a chatbot, the chances of being asked will rise significantly!

title: 1  Installing R and RStudio
text:
Step 1: Install R
Go to the R download site, CRAN: https://cran.r-project.org/. At the top of the page there are three links, one for each operating system. Click the one for your computer.
You won’t open R itself again after this: from now on, RStudio will start it for you.

title: 1  Installing R and RStudio
text:
The download links at the top of the CRAN homepage.



WindowsmacOS



On the ‘R for Windows’ page, click base (or install R for the first time).

Click the large Download R-4.x.x for Windows link at the top of the next page. The numbers will depend on the latest version; always get the latest one.
Open the downloaded file (it’s called something like R-4.x.x-win.exe) and click through the installer. The default options are all fine, so you can just keep clicking Next and then Finish.




First, check which kind of Mac you have. Click the Apple menu in the top-left corner of the screen, and choose About This Mac. If you see Chip: Apple M1 (or M2, M3, and so on), you have an Apple silicon Mac. If you see Processor: … Intel, you have an Intel Mac.
On the ‘R for macOS’ page, under Latest release, download the right file for your Mac: the one with arm64 in its name for Apple silicon, or the one with x86_64 in its name for Intel.

Open the downloaded .pkg file and click through the installer, keeping the default options.

title: 1  Installing R and RStudio
text:
Step 2: Install RStudio
Go to https://docs.posit.co/ide/user/download.html. The page should detect your computer and show a ‘Recommended for you’ box, with a button such as Download for macOS or Download for Windows: click it. (On a Mac, there’s only one version, for both Apple silicon and Intel.) If the page offers the wrong version, scroll down to the list of all installers.


WindowsmacOS


Open the downloaded .exe file and click through the installer, keeping the default options. RStudio will appear in your Start menu.


Open the downloaded .dmg file. A window opens with the RStudio icon and a shortcut to your Applications folder: drag the RStudio icon onto the Applications folder.
Then open RStudio from your Applications folder (not from the window that opened from the .dmg). The first time, macOS will ask whether you’re sure you want to open an app downloaded from the internet: click Open. You can then eject the RStudio ‘disk’ in Finder and delete the .dmg file.

title: 1  Installing R and RStudio
text:
Step 3: Open RStudio
Open RStudio. You should see a window divided into three panes. On the left is the console, which starts with a message telling you which version of R is running. If you see this, R and RStudio are both installed and talking to each other.



RStudio when you open it for the first time.


Click in the console, next to the > symbol, type 1 + 1, and press Enter. R should answer with [1] 2.






Tip



If RStudio asks you to choose a version of R, or says it can’t find R, then R didn’t install properly. Go back to step 1 and run the R installer again, then restart RStudio.

title: 1  Installing R and RStudio
text:
Step 4: Install the course packages
R comes with a set of basic functions, but most of what we’ll do uses packages: free add-ons written by other R users. You only need to install each package once on your computer. Copy the following into the console, and press Enter:
install.packages(c("tidyverse", "rmarkdown", "sf", "rnaturalearth",
                   "rnaturalearthdata", "ggthemes", "patchwork",
                   "palmerpenguins"))
This downloads and installs quite a lot of software, so it can take several minutes. Lots of text will scroll past in the console, some of it in red. This is normal: red text in R isn’t always an error. Wait until the console shows the > symbol again before you do anything else.



The console when the packages have finished installing.








‘Do you want to install from sources?’



At some point R may stop and ask ‘Do you want to install from sources the packages which need compilation? (Yes/no/cancel)’. Type no and press Enter. Installing ‘from sources’ needs extra tools that you don’t have, and the version R installs instead works just as well.


To check that it worked, run this in the console:
library(tidyverse)
You should see a short list of packages with tick marks next to them, something like this. If instead you see the error there is no package called 'tidyverse', the installation didn’t finish: run the install.packages() line again.

title: 1  Installing R and RStudio
section: Step 5: Make a project folder for the course
text:
Step 5: Make a project folder for the course
For this course, you’ll keep everything (data, R Markdown files, and the reports you knit) in one folder on your computer. RStudio can manage this folder for you as a project. When you work inside a project, R automatically looks for files in that folder, so you can read in a dataset just by giving its file name.

In RStudio, click File → New Project…, then New Directory, then New Project.

Under Directory name, type cultural_analytics. Next to Create project as subdirectory of, click Browse… and choose where to put it, for example your Documents folder. Click Create Project.


RStudio will restart inside your new project. You can tell, because the project name appears in the top-right corner of the window, and the Files pane (bottom right) shows the contents of your new folder, which for now is just a file called cultural_analytics.Rproj.

Whenever you work on this course, open this project first: either double-click the cultural_analytics.Rproj file in the folder, or in RStudio click File → Open Project…, or pick it from the menu in the top-right corner. When you download a dataset for an exercise, save it (or move it) into this folder.






Tip



It’s best to make this folder somewhere that isn’t synced by OneDrive, iCloud Drive, Dropbox or Google Drive. Syncing software sometimes locks files while R is using them, which can cause strange errors. Keep your own backup copy of your work somewhere else instead.

title: 1  Installing R and RStudio
text:
Step 6: Change one setting
By default, RStudio saves everything you’ve created in a session, and quietly loads it again the next time you open it. This sounds helpful, but it means your code can end up relying on things you made earlier and then deleted from your file - and then the same code fails when you knit it, or when someone else runs it. It’s better to start each session fresh.
Click Tools → Global Options…. On the General page:

untick Restore .RData into workspace at startup
set Save workspace to .RData on exit to Never

Then click OK.

title: 1  Installing R and RStudio
text:
Check that everything works
Finally, copy this code into the console and press Enter. It loads the packages, and draws a scatter plot and a world map.
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
library(rnaturalearth)

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) + geom_point()
ggplot(ne_countries()) + geom_sf()
The charts appear in the Plots tab in the bottom-right pane. You’ll see the map first: click the left arrow at the top of the Plots tab to go back to the scatter plot. If you can see both, you’re ready for the course.

title: 1  Installing R and RStudio
text:
If something goes wrong

An error that says there is no package called '...'. That package didn’t install. Run install.packages("...") again, with the package name from the error message, and read the messages in the console to see what went wrong.
A warning that a package ‘was built under R version …’. You can ignore this. It just means the package was made with a slightly newer version of R than yours. It still works.
A warning that ‘Rtools is required to build R packages’ (Windows). You can ignore this. You only need Rtools to install packages ‘from sources’, which you don’t need to do.
You already had R or RStudio installed. Check the version: the first line of the console message when you open RStudio says which version of R you have. If it’s more than about a year old, install the latest version over it, following the steps above, and then install the packages again.
Something else. Copy the exact error message, or take a screenshot of the whole RStudio window, and bring it to the first class or post it on Brightspace. Searching the web for the exact error message often helps too.

title: 2  Introduction to R
text:
Working with this book.
In each session we’ll demonstrate and practise some basics by running code directly in your browser, in this book. You can see the content and structure of the book in the sidebar on the left-hand side. Each week of the course has a ‘part’ (this week is ‘Introduction to R & Data Analysis 1’), and each part has a number of chapters, which you can identify because they are numbered. You can switch to a new part of the book by clicking in the sidebar, or you can use the link at the bottom of each page to go to the next chapter.
For the first few weeks, we’ll learn the basics through live code cells which are embedded in the book itself, and running in your browser. Later, we’ll switch to an IDE (Integrated Development Environment) which will give us a ‘real world’ system to practise in.






Warning



Code written in a browser like this will not be saved if you close or refresh the page. Only use it for practising the basics!


You can identify these ‘live’ code cells as they look like this:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
If you see the ‘Installing package…’ or ‘Loading package…’ message, this means that the programming language is doing some work behind the scenes to get everything working. When it’s finished, it will be replaced by a ‘Run Code’ button.

Features of the code cell
The code cell itself has a few features:








Feature
Image
Description




Run Code button

Pressing this will run, or execute, the code in the cell.


The code input box

Errors
The code above is a good way to demonstrate two more features of coding in R in the manner. First, instead of printing a result, the code above printed some text in red directly below the code cell. This is an indication that the code has not run and has instead given an error. Red text can also mean warnings or messages.

Errors are the most severe; they indicate that there is no way for code to run.
Warnings fall somewhat in between errors and message, and typically indicate that something has gone wrong but the code has been able to at least partially recover.
Messages are the mildest; they are way of informing users that some action has been performed on their behalf.

title: 5  R-Studio and using R Markdown
text:
R Markdown and ‘Knitting’ a Document
There are several ways to create and execute code within R studio, such as creating scripts or typing into the console (the bottom-left pane).
However, in this course, we’ll exclusively use one method: R Markdown notebooks.
These are special documents which can include code and text. Text is written using a simple format called Markdown, and code goes into special ‘cells’ within the document. Once you’re finished, you’ll tell R studio to execute all the code in the document and render it as an html file. This process is called ‘knitting’.
We’ll worry more about code in the next session, but for now, let’s just get used to creating R Markdown files, knitting them, and downloading them to your local machine so they can be sent as assignments.

Create a new markdown file
Click file -> new file -> R Markdown

If asked to install packages, just click yes, and wait a little longer.
You’ll get a pop-up with some options, as there are several types of markdown documents you can make. The defaults are OK; you don’t need to change anything, so just click OK. You can add a title here if you like, but it is easy to do later.

At the moment, there is some sample text and code in the document.
At the top of the document is some formatted text which looks like this:

This is called a yaml header. It contains information about your document, and it needs to remain here for the notebook to work. You can use this yaml header to edit the title of your report: just edit the text within the quotation marks which now reads ‘Untitled’.
You should delete the rest of the text in the document: highlight and delete the rest of the contents of the notebook, using delete/backspace.


Type some text
Type some text. There are two ways of doing this. You can use the source editor, which is the default view. You can switch between Source and Visual using the button above.

In the source editor, use markdown. This is a very simple coding language used to render text on the internet. There are codes for bold, italics, headings. You can add images etc. You can switch between the two at any time.

In the visual editor, use the menu items to format your text. For example bold, italics, headings. You can use the drop-down menu to add images, tables, and so forth, as you would with word processor software such as Word or Google docs.







Warning



Be careful when switching between the Source and Visual editors, as this is an easy way to get weird formatting errors. A common example of this is accidentally adding the markdown code for a title (e.g ##) in the Visual mode instead of the Source mode.




Save the file
In order to render/knit the file, it needs to be saved first.
Click file, save, and give it a name.


Naming conventions.
In this course, you will be required to use good naming conventions. Save the file with an appropriate name which communicates the most important information about the file: who created it, and what it contains.
Once you have done this, you’ll see a new .Rmd file appear in the file browser, in the bottom-right pane:




Knit the document
Now, we’ll render the document. When a document is rendered, it restarts the R engine, runs through the code, and outputs the document. In this case, it will be very quick, as we haven’t written any code.
Click the Knit button (with the ball of wool icon) at the top of the editor. You can also click the small arrow next to it, and choose Knit to HTML. This will create a new file in your folder.

The knitted html file will preview in a new window. You can close this.
More importantly, there is now a new file in the file browser:


The file ending in .html is the knitted output of the markdown.
The file ending in .Rmd is the ‘source code’ of the final file.



Zip the files
To submit R Markdown files as assignments in Brightspace, you’ll need to put both the html output and the ‘raw’ markdown file into a single .zip file.
First, open your project folder on your computer: in the Files pane, click the More menu (the gear icon), and then Show Folder in New Window.

Select both the .Rmd file and the .html file (hold down Ctrl on Windows, or Cmd on a Mac, and click each one). Then:

Windows: right-click one of the selected files, and choose Compress to ZIP file (on older versions of Windows: Send to → Compressed (zipped) folder).
macOS: right-click one of the selected files, and choose Compress 2 Items. This makes a file called Archive.zip.

Rename the .zip file with a sensible name, and then you can upload it directly to Brightspace.
This is the format we will use for every assignment, so it’s worth getting the hang of it!


Upload to Brightspace
Upload the .zip file to Brightspace in the assignment area.

Exercise 1: work with variables and mathematical operations





Illustration of book sizes. Found here



You’re working on a book history project, and you’re interested in finding out more about the most-used book formats. When books were still made by hand (up until the beginning of the nineteenth century), books were made by printing on a standard sized sheet of paper and then folding the paper a number of times to make the pages. This process determined the different sizes, or formats, of books.
The largest size (a single fold) was called folio, followed by quarto, octavo, and duodecimo. (you might have heard of the Shakespeare ‘first folio’, which is so named because it was the first time Shakespeare was published in folio format - individual plays had previously been published as quarto).








Why does this matter?



In the study of the book (bibliography), determining the format is important: folio-sized books were reserved for important and expensive publications which were meant to last. In a real-world example, we could do this on a large dataset of information from a book catalogue, to look for patterns and changes over time. In that case, we would usually do a similar calculation, but over a whole column of numbers.




Steps

In a first code cell, create two variables, called book_height and book_width. Set each to a number: make up some realistic values for book height and width in millimetres.
In a new code cell, write code that will multiply them together, and save this as a variable book_area.
Now, let’s calculate the area of a typical folio book. A full sheet of paper measured 500 x 740 mm. In a new code cell, write code to calculate the area, in millimetres squared, of a folio page (remember the full sheet of paper is also folded in half to make the page).

Any book which has an area equal or larger than this is considered folio size.

In a new code cell, write code to do this comparison using the variables created above.

See below for the answer if you get stuck:


Code
book_height <- 250

book_width <- 180

book_area <- book_height * book_width

folio_area <- (500 * 740) / 2 # the width multiplied by the height, divided by two

book_area >= folio_area # check if book area is greater than or equal to folio_area.

Dataframes
One of the data types that we can work with in R is a dataframe. This is an object with rows and columns, like a spreadsheet in Microsoft Excel or Google Sheets.
Almost all structured data comes in this form, and for the rest of the course the datasets we’ll work with will all be dataframes. Later, you’ll learn how to import dataframes from your computer or online sources. For now, we’ll work with a dataframe which has been loaded into the memory of the programming language in this book.
Remember earlier this week we could create variables, such as x = 5 or y = 10? We could also call these objects (in our code’s memory x is an object with the value 5). A dataframe can also be stored with a name and manipulated as an object.
Usually, you need to load dataframes from external sources, such as a spreadsheet file, or from a file online, or by web scraping, and so forth. In this book environment, there is already a dataframe with the name titanic_df. The object titanic_df is a spreadsheet-like object containing one row for each passenger on the Titanic. The columns in this object contain information about the passengers, such as their name, age, passenger class and so forth.
The simplest way to look at a dataframe or any other object is to enter it in a code cell and run the code, just as we did with simper variables like numbers or vectors. Try it by running the code below:
It’s worth familiarising yourself with how a dataframe looks when you print it in the book like this, because it will help to understand the results of your actions. When you work in RStudio, the interface is specially set up for viewing dataframes, where they will be easier to read, like in spreadsheet software such as Excel.

The Titanic Dataset
It’s good to understand a bit more about the dataset which we’ll use quite a lot for examples, exercises and visualisations over the next few weeks. You can find out more about the dataset here. It contains information on 1,309 passengers who sailed on the titanic, such as their age, sex, and the fare paid. The column names are the following:

survived: either 1 or 0, indicating whether the passenger survived or not.
pclass: either 1, 2, or 3, listing the passenger class
name: the full name of the passenger
sex: the sex of the passenger, either male or female
age: the age of the passenger, sometimes given with decimals
sibsp: the number of siblings or spouses on the same ticket
parch: the number of parents or children on the same ticket
ticket: the unique ticket number (like an order number)
fare: the fare paid (for the entire ticket)
cabin: the cabin number

Each individual is a separate row in the dataset, but the ticket numbers are often repeated. This is because one ticket could cover multiple people, for example a family. The fare given is for the ticket as a whole.

title: 7  Data Analysis 1
text:
Tidyverse
Most of the work in this course will use a set of packages developed for R called the ‘tidyverse’. These enhance and improve a large range of R functions with a more intuitive syntax, particularly for working with dataframes and for visualisation. The Tidyverse is really a ‘family’ of individual packages for sorting, filtering and plotting data frames. Almost all of the functions we use from now on will come from this family.

title: 7  Data Analysis 1
text:
Functions
The way we’ll do operations on dataframes is to use functions on them. A function is a pre-made piece of code which does a particular task on a piece of data. The task might be an algorithm or mathematical process, and the data might be something as simple as a number, or it could be a dataframe, which we will be mostly working with here. You have already used the print() and nchar() functions, earlier this week.
When we manipulate dataframes, or create visualisations, we will almost always use one or more of these functions (you can also write your own, but we won’t cover that on this course). It’s important to understand how to use a function in R for this course.

Function names
A function in R is stored as a single ‘string’ (a sequence of characters with no spaces) followed by an open and closed set of brackets. A function called ‘function’ will look like this in R: function().
Most of the functions we work with will have logical-sounding names, usually verbs. For example, the function to filter a dataset is called filter(), and the function to select certain columns is called select().


Function arguments
Some functions work entirely within themselves and don’t need any further information, but usually, we’ll need to supply at least a few things to make a function work. The elements that we supply to the function are called ‘arguments’. Each argument in a function is placed within the brackets of the function, and each one must be separated by a comma.
Typically, the functions we use will make a change to a dataframe (such as filter or select). For these kinds of functions, we usually need to supply at least two things:

The dataframe to be worked on
The further instructions on what the function should do specifically to the dataframe.

Sometimes, we will also need to set parameters (basically options), which are more specific instructions on how the function should act.
It’s good to familiarise yourself with how a function looks and how you can use them. This is a typical example:

Different functions will need different instructions, depending on what they do. The code above runs the filter() function on the dataset titanic_df, with the instruction that the data in the age column should equal 50.

Here, we use the function slice_max on the dataframe titanic_df (we’ll learn what this does later). This time we have to set two parameters. Parameters have specific names and we set their values using an single equal sign. Here, we have to set the order_by parameter, which we have set to the column age, and we have to set the n parameter, which we set to 10.






Warning



Notice in the first function we used Age == 50, and in the second function we used order_by = Age? This is because they mean different things. In R, a double equal sign (==) means ‘check if this is equal to’. A single equal sign (=) means ‘set this to the value of’.
When setting the value of a parameter, we always use a single equal sign. Using the wrong one is an easy mistake to make and can be good to check when troubleshooting!

title: 11  The pipe operator
text:
Piping
You can see that in many cases, we might want to do multiple operations to a dataset, one after another. In the previous example we wanted to look at the oldest passengers for each sex. In that case, it would have been nice to use select after arrange to keep only the columns we were interested in looking at.
One way to do this is to wrap the arrange() verb in a select() verb, like this:
This can get confusing pretty quickly, because it looks messy and it’s difficult to tell which order things happen in. This is important in some circumstances - for instance you might get different results if you summarise some data before or after you filter it.
R has a special command, called a pipe, which can be used to make much more readable code. The pipe will take a dataframe and pass it along to another function. This can be done multiple times: the code will do one operation, then the resulting dataframe will be passed on to the next function, and so forth. The pipe command is the following two characters: |>.

title: 14  Filtering data
text:
Filtering data with filter()
One of the most useful things you will do in data analysis is to filter to only look at certain parts of your data. This is done with a verb called filter(). Filter is very powerful because you can set it to filter for any number of conditions or patterns.
The filter() function keeps only certain rows in a dataframe, based on a condition which you set within the function. This is very useful when working with data visualisations, because often you will want to focus on a small amount of the data, or perhaps a single category.
In the filter function, the first argument is the data to be filtered. The second is the column you want to look at, and finally, a condition (or multiple conditions). The function will return every row where that condition is true.
Remember in the first week when we looked at comparisons, such as ==, <,> and %in%? One important way these are used are to set the conditions for a filter.
With filter, need the dataset followed by the column you want to look at, followed by the comparison. The left side of the comparison will generally be a column from your dataframe, followed by a comparison symbol, followed by a value. You can use multiple comparisons using &.
We can use filter to return rows where the text in a column matches a given string:

Check your understanding
These questions are in the same style as the exam. Try to answer each one before running any code - then use the code cell to check your answer.
1. Which of these two will return more rows, and why?
titanic_df |> filter(pclass == 1, sex == 'female')

titanic_df |> filter(pclass == 1 | sex == 'female')

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.






Answer





The second. A comma (like &) means and: a row is kept only if the passenger was in first class and female. | means or: a row is kept if the passenger was in first class, or female, or both - so it includes all first-class men and all women in second and third class as well.



2. This code gives the error object 'C' not found. What’s wrong?
titanic_df |> filter(embarked == C)






Answer





C needs quotation marks: filter(embarked == 'C'). Without them, R thinks C is the name of an object (or a column), rather than a piece of text to compare against.



3. You want to keep only passengers who were younger than 10 or older than 60. Which of these is correct?

titanic_df |> filter(age < 10, age > 60)
titanic_df |> filter(age < 10 | age > 60)
titanic_df |> filter(age %in% c(10, 60))







Answer





b. (a) asks for passengers younger than 10 and older than 60 at the same time, which is impossible, so it returns no rows. (c) only returns passengers aged exactly 10 or exactly 60.

section: Putting it together: “women and children first”?
text:
Putting it together: “women and children first”?
The story goes that as the Titanic sank, the rule was “women and children first”. Overall, 38% of the 1,309 passengers survived: 73% of the women, but only 19% of the men. But did class matter as well as sex? With group_by() and summarise() we can check this ourselves, from the raw passenger list.
The survived column is 1 if the passenger survived and 0 if they didn’t. That means the mean of survived is the share who survived: the mean of 1, 1, 0 and 0 is 0.5, or 50%. So we can calculate a survival rate for each group with mean(survived):

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Read down the survival column. 97% of women in first class survived, but only 49% of women in third class. For men, it was 34% in first class and 15% in second and third. A woman in third class had about the same chance as a man in first: class mattered as well as sex.

title: 21  Joins
text:
left_join(), right_join(), inner_join()
Another set of commands we’ll use quite often in this course are the join() ‘family’. Joins are a very powerful but simple way of selecting certain subsets of data, and adding information from multiple tables together.
Remember the titanic dataset had a column ‘embarked’, which contained either Q, S or C, which told where the passenger got on?
Let’s say we wanted to display the full name of the embarking location, plus some other information. We have another dataset, called locations_df, which contains the code and the equivalent full name, plus the country name and coordinates of the location. You can see what this looks like by running the cell below:
We can combine these two tables of information, so that they are merged, or joined together - the result will be that the correct extra information for each place code will be added to the titanic_df data.
This is done using a set of functions called joins.
In R, we can do these joins using the functions left_join(), right_join() and inner_join(). These are variations on the same thing, and they differ by the way that they merge the two datasets together.
Joins need a common key, a column which allows the join to match the data tables up. It’s important that these are unique (a person’s name makes a bad key by itself, for example, because it’s likely more than one person will share the same name). Usually, we use codes as the join keys. If the columns containing the join keys have different names (as ours do), specify them using the syntax below:

title: 22  Tidying data with pivot_longer()
text:
Reshaping data
The final function we’ll learn in this section on data science is called pivot_longer(). The use of this might seem a bit abstract at first, but I hope it is something you will find very useful in the long run, because it will allow you to apply your data wrangling skills to a much wider pool of datasets.

title: 22  Tidying data with pivot_longer()
text:
Data terminology
To understand what it does, we need to back up a little bit. First of all, a bit of terminology about datasets:

variables can be thought of as the label of a fact, such as eye colour, hair colour, city of birth, and so forth.
observations are individual instances of that fact, usually a single thing recorded about something. For example, you could record my eye colour and the observation would be ‘The eye colour of Yann Ryan is…’
Values are the actual measurements for that fact: in this case, the value for this observation would be blue.



Wide and long data
Tabular datasets can usually be described in one of two formats: wide or long.

Wide datasets are where observations can be in columns. For example, if you had a dataset of a group of employment rates and the value for 2017 is in one column, the value for 2018 in the next, and so forth.



Long datasets are where each observation is in a separate row, like this:


In this case, each individual fact (for example, ‘the employment rate of Belgium in 2017’) has a separate row.
Recording data in this second method is desirable for data analysis (the first is more useful when looking at a table in a spreadsheet programme), as it makes it much easier to work with. Data in this format is also known as tidy.

title: 22  Tidying data with pivot_longer()
text:
Tidy data
Tidy data is data where:

Each variable is in its own column.
Each observation is in its own row
Each value is in its own cell.

As an example of a ‘wide’ dataset, there is a dataset called gapminder_population loaded into memory. View it by running the cell below:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
This dataset contains population records for countries in Europe. You can see that each country is a separate row, and each year is a separate column. This is not tidy data, because each year is actually a separate observation, and should in its own row.

title: 22  Tidying data with pivot_longer()
text:
pivot_longer()
To reshape this to the more useful format, we can use a new function called pivot_longer(). This takes a dataset and a specified set of columns, and reshapes them so that each of these columns now have their own row, repeating the information where needed.
The function has a number of important arguments:

The dataset to use (or one passed from the pipe)
cols which lists the columns to reshape. The columns can be selected using the same methods as the select() function, meaning they can be selected by position, name, and so forth.
names_to: what you would like to call the column containing the new variable.
values_to: what you would like to call the new values.


Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
See the shape of the data? It now contains far more rows, one for each observation (the population for a given country in a particular year): 30 countries × 12 years = 360 rows.
Notice that the new year column is text (<chr>), not a number. Column names are always text, so that’s what pivot_longer() gives us. It means that when you filter on the year, you should put it in quotes: year == '2007'.
Once the data is long, all the verbs you already know work on it, because the year is now a column you can filter, group and sort by.

title: 24  Data challenge 2: What did Hemingway read?
text:
The data
Shakespeare and Company was an English-language bookshop and lending library in Paris, run by Sylvia Beach from 1919 to 1941. It published James Joyce’s Ulysses in 1922. Its members included Ernest Hemingway, Gertrude Stein, Simone de Beauvoir and Joyce himself, along with thousands of ordinary Parisian readers. Beach kept a card for each member, recording every book they borrowed. The Shakespeare and Company Project at Princeton has transcribed these cards. This means we know what Hemingway was reading, and when.
The datasets are on Princeton Data Commons. Download these four csv files (they’re also on Brightspace) and save them in your project folder:
You’ll see a warning about “parsing issues” when you read in the books file. You can ignore it.

title: 24  Data challenge 2: What did Hemingway read?
text:
SCoData_events_v2.0_2025.csv: one row per event at the library: a borrow, a subscription, a purchase and so on. Members are identified in member_ids, and books in item_uri. Authors appear in item_authors, written surname first.
SCoData_books_v2.0_2025.csv: one row per book, identified by uri, with information such as genre_category.
SCoData_members_v2.0_2025.csv: one row per member, identified by id, with information such as gender and nationalities.
SCoData_book_creators_v2.0_2025.csv: one row per author (and editor or translator), with their gender. The sort_name column uses the same surname-first format as item_authors.

title: 24  Data challenge 2: What did Hemingway read?
section: Part 1: get to know the events
text:
Part 1: get to know the events

Load the tidyverse. Read the four files into R, and save them as events, books, members and creators. (events has 35,551 rows)
Use count() to see the different kinds of event in the event_type column. Which is the most common? (Borrow: 21,063)
Make a new dataframe called borrows. It should contain only the borrowing events, and only the columns member_ids, member_names, start_date, item_uri, item_title and item_authors.
Some library cards were shared by more than one person, such as a married couple. These rows list several members in member_ids, separated by a semicolon (;). Some books also have several authors, separated in the same way. We’ll remove both kinds of row, because they would get in the way of our joins later. Add these two lines to your code for borrows:

  filter(!str_detect(member_ids, ";")) |>
  filter(!str_detect(item_authors, ";"))
borrows should now have 18,475 rows. The ! means “not”, so these lines keep only the rows without a semicolon. The second line also drops rows where item_authors is empty, such as magazines. Why do you think that happens? (Hint: what does str_detect() give for a missing value, and what does filter() do with it?)

The start_date column is text, written as year-month-day (1925-10-22). Use mutate() and case_when() to add a decade column. Combine them with str_detect() and the ^ anchor to check how each date begins: str_detect(start_date, "^192") ~ "1920s", and so on for the 1930s and 1940s. Then count the borrows in each decade. (1930s: 10,520)

title: 24  Data challenge 2: What did Hemingway read?
text:
Part 2: Hemingway’s library card

Filter borrows to the rows for "Ernest Hemingway". How many books did he borrow? (89)
Which author did he borrow most often? Use count() and slice_max(). (Turgenev, Ivan: 12)
Arrange his borrows by start_date. What are the first five things on his card? (Hemingway joined in 1921, but his recorded borrowing only begins in October 1925.)
Now keep only his Turgenev borrows. Look at the title and date of the third one. Then look up when Hemingway wrote his own short novel, and what he called it. 🤯
Use %in% to filter borrows to four famous members: "Ernest Hemingway", "James Joyce", "Gertrude Stein" and "Simone de Beauvoir". Count how many books each of them borrowed. (Joyce: 77)
Joyce’s own books were in the library too. Use str_detect(item_authors, "^Joyce, James") to find borrows of books written by Joyce, and count them by title. Which was borrowed most? (A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man: 55)
crumbs: 24  Data challenge 2: What did Hemingway read?

title: 24  Data challenge 2: What did Hemingway read?
text:
Part 3: reading diets
What kinds of books did each of these four writers borrow?

Take your four famous members from Part 2. Use left_join() to add the genre_category column from books. Join item_uri in borrows to uri in books. (Tip: select() just the two columns you need from books inside the join.)
Some books have more than one genre, such as Fiction;Poetry. So we can’t just count() the genre column. Instead, use group_by() and summarise() to make four new columns, one for each genre, that count how many borrowed books mention it. Here is the line for fiction:

fiction = sum(str_detect(genre_category, "Fiction"), na.rm = TRUE)
Do the same for "Nonfiction", "Poetry" and "Drama". Save the result as diets. (Hemingway: 46 fiction, 38 nonfiction)

Hold on, there’s a trap here. str_detect(genre_category, "Fiction") also matches "Nonfiction", doesn’t it? Check whether that’s true. (Hint: are capital letters treated the same as lower case?)
diets is a wide table, with one column per genre. Use pivot_longer() to make it tidy, with columns called genre and borrows.
Using group_by() and mutate(), work out what share (percentage) of each writer’s borrowing went to each genre. Which writer was almost entirely a fiction reader, and which one read mostly nonfiction? (Stein: 86% fiction; Joyce: 62% nonfiction) Joyce was writing Finnegans Wake at the time. Why might he have been borrowing so much nonfiction?
crumbs: 24  Data challenge 2: What did Hemingway read?

title: 24  Data challenge 2: What did Hemingway read?
section: Part 4: did women read women writers?
text:
Part 4: did women read women writers?
Now the big question. In home exercise 4 we looked at how much dialogue women get in films. Here we can ask a similar question about readers: did women and men at Shakespeare and Company choose authors of their own gender?

We need to join creators to borrows, matching item_authors to sort_name. But first, check the join key: use count() on sort_name and filter for any name that appears more than once. What do you find? Look the duplicate up in creators. Remember what the Joins chapter said about names being bad keys. (one name, twice)
Make a cleaned version of creators without the duplicate. Keep the novelist born in 1843, and remove the row whose id is "james-henry-2". Keep only sort_name and gender, and rename gender to author_gender. (You can rename inside select(), like this: select(sort_name, author_gender = gender).)
Do the same with members: keep id, and rename gender to reader_gender.
Join both of these to borrows with left_join(), and save the result as borrows_full. Check that it still has the same number of rows as borrows. (18,475) If it has more, your duplicate isn’t gone!
Filter to rows where both author_gender and reader_gender are "Female" or "Male". Count each combination of reader gender and author gender. Then use group_by(reader_gender) and mutate() to turn the counts into percentages. (Women readers: 29.1% women authors; men: 14.6%)
Did this change over time? Repeat the calculation by decade instead of reader gender. (1920s: 17.7% women authors; 1940s: 31.1%) Note that the library closed in 1941, so “1940s” really means 1940 and 1941.
Which women authors were borrowed most? Which were borrowed most by men? (Virginia Woolf both times)
Export borrows_full with write_csv(). We’ll come back to this data in data challenge 3, when we turn it into charts.

Write a short paragraph (three or four sentences) answering the question in the heading of Part 4. Is there anything in how the data was made (whose cards survived, how gender was recorded, which books we removed) that should make us careful about the answer?

Now count the total borrows of every member in borrows. Why might Alice Killen not really be Hemingway’s “reading twin”? How could you make a fairer comparison?

text:
The data
Today we will use a dataset from an article written for The Pudding: Hannah Anderson and Matt Daniels, “Film Dialogue from 2,000 screenplays, Broken Down by Gender and Age”. Have a look at the article first: it asks the same questions as these exercises.
The article used screenplays to understand the gender balance of films, and how it has changed over time. The data covers 2,000 films from 1929 to 2015. It comes in three files:

character_list5.csv: one row per character, with the script_id of the film, the character’s name, the number of words they speak, their gender and their age.
meta_data7.csv: one row per film, with the same script_id, plus the imdb_id, title, year and gross (box office takings). You can ignore the lines_data column.
imdb_genre.csv: one row per film, with its genres, taken from IMDb. It doesn’t have the script_id, but its tconst column holds the same IMDb ID as imdb_id in the metadata.

Dialogue is measured in words, not lines.

Exercises

Exercise 1: load the data
Code: load the tidyverse package with library(), and read all three files into R. Save them as objects called characters, meta and genres.


Exercise 2: join the characters to the films
Code: use left_join() to join meta to characters, using script_id as the key, so that each character has the title and year of their film alongside them. Save the result as dialogue, and show how many rows it has with nrow(dialogue). (23,048)

Exercise 3: how is gender recorded?
Code: use count() on the gender column of dialogue. (Three values: f 6,911, m 16,132 and ? 5)
Write: what do you think each of the three values means?


Exercise 4: the overall balance
Code: using group_by() and summarise(), calculate the total number of words spoken by each gender, across all the films. (f 5,877,657 words)
Write: roughly what share of all the dialogue is spoken by women? You can work it out from your result with a calculator, or try it in R with mutate(). (About 28%)


Exercise 5: one row per film
Make a new dataframe, called films, with one row for each film, and two columns counting the words spoken by women and by men in that film.
This needs a trick. First, use mutate() and if_else() to make two new columns: female_words, which holds the character’s words if they are female and 0 if not, and male_words, which does the same for men. Then group by film and add up those two columns with summarise().
Code: copy this code into your file, run it and look at the result. (2,000 rows)
films <- dialogue |>
  mutate(female_words = if_else(gender == 'f', words, 0),
         male_words = if_else(gender == 'm', words, 0)) |>
  group_by(script_id, imdb_id, title, year) |>
  summarise(female = sum(female_words),
            male = sum(male_words))
Code: run count(meta, title), and arrange the result so the largest counts are at the top.
Write: answer these two questions.

Why do we group by script_id, and not just by title? Use the result of count() to explain.
Why do we also put imdb_id, title and year in the group_by(), if script_id is already enough to make one row per film?

Code: add two new columns to films with mutate(), and save the result:

prop_female: the share of the dialogue spoken by women. This is the female words divided by the female and male words added together.
balance: use case_when() to make this ‘more female’ if there are more female words than male words, ‘more male’ if there are more male words, and ‘equal’ if they are exactly the same.

Then count the values in balance. (304 more female, 1,695 more male, 1 equal)

Write: which film is it?

Tip



All the Star Wars titles start with ‘Star Wars’. You can find them with str_detect(), from the optional chapter on text patterns: filter(str_detect(title, 'Star Wars')).


Write: which Star Wars film has the highest share of female dialogue, and which the lowest? How do they compare with the share for all films that you found in exercise 4? (The highest is The Force Awakens, at about 28%)

Which genres have the most female dialogue?

title: 27  Data Visualisation Basics
text:
Data Visualisation Principles
This week, we’ll begin working with data visualisations. We’ll introduce in a very general sense the different ways we can draw things with data visualisation software. We won’t think too much about the specifics of making charts for different purposes - just get used to the general syntax and most common chart types.

title: 27  Data Visualisation Basics
text:
Aims of Information Design
To begin with, we should think about the purpose of data visualisation. Essentially, the purpose is to aid cognition, usually of large-scale or complex data which otherwise is difficult to grasp. Some examples of how it aids cognition include using infovis to:

Understand, explore and remember information
Take in large amounts of data at once
Make comparisons
Read millions of data points or understand complex structures (e.g. hierarchies or networks)
Understand temporal information, e.g. logic of going from earlier to later time

The reason data visualisation works is because our brains tend to make judgements about values based on visual elements. For example, if given two circles, one small and one big, and are asked which we think represents the larger value, you would likely pick the bigger one.
Similarly, we associate ‘hotter’ colours with larger values than colder ones.
We associate transparency or opacity with strength. And so forth..
We can use these principles in data visualisations. By mapping data to these visual elements, we can aid in the understanding of a given dataset by viewers.
Next week, we’ll take a closer look at some of the psychological principles behind why these work. For today, we’ll focus on the pratical aspects.

title: 27  Data Visualisation Basics
section: Mapping Data to Geometries and Aesthetics
text:
Mapping Data to Geometries and Aesthetics
These visual elements can be broken down into geometries and aesthetics. Geometries are the basic geometric shapes, like circles, points, lines, and so forth. Aesthetics are the features of those shapes, like size, colour, and position.
In the next two parts of the chapter, we’ll look at the typical geometries available to us.
On this page we concentrate on the aesthetics.

Aesthetics
There are many possible aesthetics, but some of the most commonly-found in infovis are:

Another important one not pictured here is transparency.
We can use these aesthetics to tell lots of different stories within our data. For example, we can use them to indicate the magnitude of a value, to draw attention to different categories, or simply to highlight information we wish the viewer to pay attention to.
So how can we use each of these?


Discrete vs continuous aesthetics
Most aesthetics work on either discrete or continuous scales. We’ll learn more about scales in an upcoming session, but for now, you can think of scales as either representing sequential numbers (continuous) or distinct numbers or categories (discrete or categorical).
Which scale is suitable depends on the kind of data. Continuous data are things like age, height, or population, where the data might be any number from across a range. Discrete data are numbers where the value can only be one number or another, and not any value in between. Categorical data are data with a limited number of unordered categories, like gender, country, and so forth. A fourth type, ordinal, are categories where there is some inherent order, for example months of the year.



The four main data types, with examples from the Titanic passenger list. The bottom row shows which aesthetics suit each kind of data.








Note



We have come across most of these data types in R already: values such as age in the passenger list are continuous (age could also be discrete if it was stored in full years); gender and place of embarking are both categorical. Categorical data are usually stored in columns with the string type (<str>), whereas continuous are stored as double (<dbl>). Discrete values may be stored as integers (<int>). Ordinal data in R is stored in a special data type, called a factor. Factors are variables that have a fixed and known set of possible values, and can be inherently ordered. We won’t really delve into factors on this course, but there are some situations where they are useful, for example if you want to reorder elements of a data visualisation.


Some aesthetics only work on one or the other (shapes can only represent categories, for instance). In other cases, the scale will work differently depending on whether it is applied to a discrete or continuous set of data. In the example of colour, below, a categorical scale is usually represented by distinct, unrelated colours, whereas a continuous scale is sequential range, running from yellow to green.
The difference between continuous and discrete scales on the colour aesthetic


Key aesthetics
Below are the aesthetics you’ll use most often in data visualisation, with some examples. The visualisations are made using the Nobel Prize dataset, containing information on every laureate and prize awarded since 1901. We’ve summarised it here to one row per prize category (Chemistry, Economic Sciences, Literature, Peace, Physics, and Physiology or Medicine), giving the number of laureates, the percentage who were women, and the average age at the time of the award.






Note



Worth bearing in mind while we use this dataset: it isn’t a neutral record of scientific or literary merit. Who gets nominated, who gets recognised, and whose contributions get overlooked (particularly women, and researchers outside a handful of countries) are all shaped by the historical biases of the institutions doing the nominating. A dataset like this rewards exactly the kind of critical, contextual reading that a humanities background gives you - the numbers alone don’t tell the whole story.


You can view the code I’ve used to make the plots, which might be useful later, as a reference.

Position
All data visualisations need to be positioned in some kind of space. In this course, that space will be 2D, but 3D visualisations are also possible. These are generally given as x and y coordinates. In the example below, position is used to highlight a relationship between two variables. This dataset graphs the average age at the time of the award on the x axis and the percentage of laureates who were women on the y axis, for each prize category.
The resulting scatterplot shows a relationship between the two variables: categories which tend to honour older laureates (Economic Sciences, Physics) also tend to have a much lower share of women than categories such as Peace and Literature.


Code
nobel_summary |>
  ggplot(aes(x = avg_age, y = pct_female)) +
  geom_point()











Size
Size is often mapped to amounts or magnitude (we naturally understand that these two things map together). If we take our chart above and map the size variable to the number of laureates in each category, the viewer will grasp intuitively that larger sizes equal a larger number of prizes given out. To make this relationship even clearer, we should include a legend.


Code
nobel_summary |>
  ggplot(aes(x = avg_age, y = pct_female, size = n)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 10) +
  labs(size = "Number of laureates")











Colour
Colour is a very useful aesthetic and can have many uses. One key one is to group data together, for example mapping the colour to the prize category. This helps a user to quickly see differences in the data between the categories.


Code
nobel_summary |>
  ggplot(aes(x = avg_age, y = pct_female, size = n, color = category)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 10) +
  labs(size = "Number of laureates")











Shape
Shape can be used similarly to colour to show different groups or categories.


Code
nobel_summary |>
  ggplot(aes(x = avg_age, y = pct_female, size = n, shape = category)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 10) +
  labs(size = "Number of laureates")











Linetype/width
Linetype isn’t so widely used in scatterplots, but can be used in other types to distinguish between groups or categories. Here, we count the number of laureates awarded per decade, for a few of the prize categories:


Code
nobel_df |>
  filter(category %in% c('Physics', 'Chemistry', 'Peace')) |>
  mutate(decade = floor(award_year / 10) * 10) |>
  group_by(decade, category) |>
  summarise(n = n(), .groups = 'drop') |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_line(aes(x = decade, y = n, linetype = category)) +
  labs(title = "Laureates per Decade", subtitle = "Selected categories, 1900s-2020s") +
  theme_bw()











Transparency
Transparency can be mapped to data, but it is more useful used as a way to help with ‘overplotting’: when shapes are drawn on top of each other and difficult to distinguish. Here, we set the opacity to 50% (and add an outline), to make it possible to see the points which overlap with each other.


Code
nobel_summary |>
  ggplot(aes(x = avg_age, y = pct_female, size = n, fill = category)) +
  geom_point(alpha = .5, pch = 21, color = 'black') +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 10) +
  labs(size = "Number of laureates")

title: 28  Using ggplot2
text:
The ggplot2 package
R has a very widely-used plotting library called ggplot2, and this is what we will use to pass our data to various geometries and aesthetics to make plots. ggplot2 is very customiseable - it will let you create almost anything as long as you can feed it data and tell it what it should draw with it.
The basis of all ggplot2 visualisations is a function called ggplot(). Think of this as the foundation of your visualisation. You’ll tell the ggplot() function what data it should use and which attributes of that data it should map to specific aesthetics.

title: 28  Using ggplot2
text:
Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.


The Grammar of Graphics
This uses a philosophy of visualisation called the ‘grammar of graphics’ (hence the ‘gg’ in the name). Essentially, this encompasses a set of rules by which we can construct visualisations, using a standard set of terms and features. Every type of of visualisation in ggplot uses this same set of grammar rules, making it very easy to make many different chart types with very little extra code.
It’s best to think of this grammar of graphics in terms of layers. We start with the function ggplot, and then supply a dataset and map this data to aesthetics : you tell ggplot how to map your numeric data to different visual features like shapes, size, and colours. The next layer is one or more geometries: these are the basic visual shapes like bars, points, and lines which make up data visualisations. Optionally you can supply scales, and other elements like facets.



By Allison Horst, CC-BY-4.0

title: 28  Using ggplot2
text:
Demonstration - making a bar chart
It’s easier to demonstrate how it works. Before you use the package, you’ll need to load it, along with the other packages we use to wrangle the data:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
As an example, let’s draw a simple bar chart using ggplot2. We want to make a simple bar chart from the Titanic dataset we have been using. The workflow looks like this: first we clean and filter the data (if necessary), then we summarise it along the lines which we want, and finally visualise it using ggplot.

Summarising the data
The first step is to produce the summary of the data we would like to visualise. Let’s try something very simple: the total number of male and female passengers. We’ll use group_by() and summarise(), as in the previous lesson:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Now we have a dataset with two columns: sex, listing either male or female, and n, containing a count of the total number of each of those passengers. We save this as a new object called df, though if you want you can simply use the ‘pipe’ and pass it along to ggplot.


Making a plot
We can make a plot by building up at least four layers:

1. ggplot()
First, create a new ggplot object with the code ggplot().


2. Data
Next, give it our new summary dataframe to work with, using the argument data = df.






Tip



You can also use the pipe operator and pass your summarised data to ggplot, without saving it as a new object. In that case, you don’t need to use the data = argument. It’s up to you what to do in your own code - I prefer to create a new object if I am using it repeatedly, as here. A good principle in coding is that if you find yourself copying and pasting the same piece of code, there’s probably a better way of doing it!




3. Aesthetics
Next we tell ggplot which columns it should use, and which aesthetics it should map these colums to. This is also done by passing the names as parameters to x and y. First, type a comma after the data = df code. Then, insert the code aes(). This tells ggplot it should interpret anything within these parentheses as aesthetic mappings. Finally, within the aes(), we’ll add the columns and aesthetics: x = sex, y = n.
The code for this looks like the following:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.


4. Geometry
At this point, we have an empty visualisation which specifies the aesthetics which should be mapped. In order to draw the correct geom, or visualisation shape, we need to add it as a layer on top of the ggplot() function.
In ggplot, a bar chart is created using the geom geom_col(). geom_col(), like all geoms, has a set of aesthetics which must be specified. In this case, we must at least specific the x and y aesthetics. These correspond to the horizontal and vertical position of the bars. When we give these aesthetics to geom_col, it will automatically figure out what to do with them.
To do this, we add a plus sign (+) followed by the geometry geom_col(), resulting in a simple bar chart:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.






Tip



Adding each layer (anything after a + sign) on a new line makes the code easier to read, though it’s not strictly necessary.


We’ll learn about the rest of the layers in upcoming sessions.



Adding other aesthetics to the chart
Each chart type will allow you to manipulate different aesthetics, depending on what makes sense for that particular shape. If you are working in RStudio, you can check all of the options for a function by typing ? before it, e.g. ?geom_col, in to the console (the bottom left pane).
For geom_col, we have to set x and y and we can optionally set alpha (the transparency), colour (the colour of the outline of the bars), fill (the colour of the inside of the bars), and linetype and linewidth (allowing you to customise the look of the outline further).

Within aes() or outside aes()?
These attributes do different things depending on whether you put them inside the aes() function or outside. When outside the aes() function, they allow you to set an attribute to an absolute value. Controlling aesthetics
To draw other chart types, we replace the geometry geom_col with others. In some cases, we will also change or add aesthetics.
Each chart type is followed by examples of the typical aesthetics which can be used with that geometry.
