section: Where should this code be placed?
text:
Where should this code be placed?
As we learned in the previous section, we can place an aesthetic either within aes() or outside it:

When we specify an aesthetic within aes(), we ask for variables from our dataset to be mapped to it. It is best to include the aes() within the ggplot() function, though it can also be placed within the geom_ function.
When we specify an aesthetic not within an aes(), it is used to map to specific values, such as setting all the points in a chart to blue. When using aesthetics like this, they should always be placed within the geom_ function.

For each aesthetic, there is an example where the aesthetic is placed within the aes() and outside it, to show the difference.

title: 29  More chart types
text:
Geom_point()
geom_point() places points on a 2D plane. It requires at least x and y coordinates within the aes(). The result is called a ‘scatterplot’.
Scatterplots are used to look for a relationship between two variables. For example: are Nobel laureates getting older? Each point is one laureate, with the year of their award on the x axis and their age at the time on the y axis:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
That’s 961 points, one for each laureate with a known birth date. The warning about 20 removed rows refers to the organisations (such as the Red Cross) that have won the Peace Prize: they have no age, so they can’t be placed on the y axis.
The cloud of points drifts upwards: in the first 25 years of the prize, the median age of a laureate was 55, and since 2000 it has been 68. A relationship is a pattern across many points, not a line through a handful.

Key aesthetics

Colour
We can set the colour of every point to a fixed value, outside the aes():

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Or map it to a column, inside the aes():

Alpha
With hundreds of points, many sit on top of each other, so we can’t see how many there are in the busiest parts of the chart. This is called overplotting. One fix is alpha, which sets the transparency, a number between 0 (invisible) and 1 (solid). Where points overlap, the colour builds up:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.


Shape
We can also change the shape. There is a set of numeric codes to select specific shapes. Here is the full set:

Shape 1, an open circle, is another way to deal with overplotting:

Like colour, shape can also be mapped to a categorical column inside the aes():

More on shapes



Notice that shapes 21 through 25 are blue with a black outline? Using these allows you to set the outline and the fill of a shape separately. If you set the shape to one of these, you can now use colour = to set the outline and fill = to set the inside colour:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.




Size
Finally, size. Outside the aes(), it makes every point bigger or smaller:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Inside the aes(), it maps a number column to the size of each point. This makes a ‘bubble chart’. Here, using nobel_summary, each point is a whole prize category, sized by its number of laureates:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

title: 29  More chart types
text:
Statistical chart types

geom_histogram
A histogram is a chart which plots the distribution of a set of values as a series of bars. Each bar represents a ‘bin’ or range of values, with the height of the bar indicating how many of the values are within that bin.
We could use it to plot the distribution of the age at which laureates received their prize, for example:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
The code for a histogram looks a little different than usual. We only set the x variable - the y position will be automatically calculated when it does the statistical transformation.
Second, you’ll notice a message underneath the plot: `stat_bin()` using `bins = 30`. Pick better value with `binwidth`. Ggplot automatically divides the data into 30 equal-sized bins by default, but this is often not the clearest way to represent the distribution. We can choose either another number of bins with the argument bins =, or choose how big each range should be with the code binwidth =.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.


geom_density
Another way to show distributions of values is using geom_density:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.


geom_boxplot
geom_boxplot shows distributions:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
A boxplot visualises the distribution of numbers (in this case, the age at which laureates in each category received their prize). The middle line is the median (the middle value, if you lined all the values up in order). The upper and lower ends of the box are the 25th and 75th percentiles, so the box contains the middle half of the values, and the dots (if any) show outliers.
This particular plot shows that Economic Sciences laureates tend to be the oldest on average and Physics laureates the youngest, while Peace laureates have by far the widest spread of ages (befitting a prize given to activists, politicians, and organisations alike, rather than for a single, slow-to-mature body of scientific work).
geom_boxplot has many attributes which can be changed, determining how the statistics are visualised. You can see these by typing ?geom_boxplot in the console.


Special case: geom_text
Geom_text will actually add the text from a column to a visualisation. This is useful if we want to label the chart itself with some values (we’ll learn better ways to annotate later in the course).
geom_text() works like any other geometry, except we must supply it with a label aesthetic:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Why have I used + 2 and round() here?


Shapes: geom_polygon, geom_segment, geom_rect
As well as these geoms which create recognisable chart types, it’s also useful to know that you can essentially create almost anything by using ggplot to draw shapes either with data or with absolute values. For example, you can make a ‘lollipop chart’ with a combination of geom_segment and geom_point, such as here to show the growth in the number of laureates per category between the 1950s and the 2010s:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Note that geom_segment needs xend and yend, as well as x and y. These shapes often have different required aesthetics.

title: 29  More chart types
text:
Small multiples with facet_wrap()
Earlier, we drew the number of laureates per decade for all six prize categories on one chart, with a different colour for each line. Here it is again:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Six lines is already quite hard to read: they cross over each other, and you have to keep looking back and forth to the legend to work out which is which.
An alternative is to draw small multiples: a series of small charts, one for each category, side by side. ggplot2 does this with facet_wrap(). Add it to the end of the chart, with a ~ (a tilde) followed by the name of the column you want to split the chart by:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Small multiples work well for two reasons:

The viewer only needs to learn to read one chart. Once they’ve understood the first panel, they can read all the others in the same way.
Every panel uses the same scales. Because the axes are the same, you can compare the panels directly: it’s easy to see that Physics, Chemistry and Medicine have grown much more than Literature or Peace, which have stayed at about one laureate a year.

Notice too that every line drops sharply at the end. That isn’t a real decline: the 2020s aren’t over yet, so the last decade only has a few years of data. It’s a good example of why you should always check what a chart is actually showing before you interpret it.
Notice that we no longer need colour or a legend: each panel is labelled with its category instead. That leaves colour free to show something else.
facet_wrap() works with any chart type. Here’s a histogram of the age at which laureates won their prize, split by category, so that we can compare the distributions:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
You can choose the number of columns (or rows) with ncol = (or nrow =). For example, facet_wrap(~ category, ncol = 1) puts all the panels in a single column, one above the other, which makes the distributions easier to compare along the age axis:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.






Free scales



By default, every panel has the same axes. You can let each panel have its own y axis with facet_wrap(~ category, scales = 'free_y'). This can be useful if some groups are much smaller than others, and you’re interested in the shape of each line rather than its size. But be careful: with free scales, panels which look similar might represent very different numbers, and the viewer can no longer compare them directly. If you use them, make sure the reader can tell.


Try it yourself: go back to the scatterplot of the age at award (age_at_award) against the year of the award (award_year), and add a separate panel for each category. Are laureates getting older in every category?

section: Choosing a chart: what am I trying to show?
text:
Choosing a chart: what am I trying to show?
You’ve now seen most of the basic chart types. But how do you choose between them?
The answer depends on two things. The first is the type of data you have: whether your variables are continuous, discrete, categorical, or ordinal (see Data Visualisation Basics). Some aesthetics and chart types only work with one or the other.
The second, and more important, is what you are trying to show: what is the story in the data, or the question you want to answer? Most charts are trying to show one of a small number of things. The cards below show the most common, with an example question from the Nobel data and the chart types (and geoms) you could use:



Amounts
How many laureates are there in each category?
Bar chart: geom_col(), geom_bar()



Ranking
Which category has the oldest laureates?
Ordered bar or lollipop chart: geom_col(), geom_segment() + geom_point()



Distribution
How old are laureates when they win?
Histogram, density plot, boxplot: geom_histogram(), geom_density(), geom_boxplot()



Relationship
Are laureates getting older over time?
Scatterplot: geom_point()



Change over time
How has the number of laureates changed by decade?
Line chart, bar chart: geom_line(), geom_col()



Part-to-whole
What share of each category’s laureates are women?
Stacked bar chart: geom_col(position = 'fill')



Comparison across groups
Has each category grown in the same way?
Small multiples: facet_wrap()



Spatial
Where were laureates born?
Map: geom_sf() (weeks 5-6)


The Financial Times has a very useful poster, the Visual Vocabulary, which does the same thing in much more detail, with dozens of chart types arranged by what they show. It’s worth keeping open while you plan your reports.
One chart type here is new: the stacked bar chart, used to show proportions. Map a category to the fill aesthetic, and add position = 'fill' to geom_col(). Each bar is then stretched to the same height, so that the y axis shows the proportion (from 0 to 1) rather than the count:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Try removing position = 'fill' and running the code again. What’s the difference, and which chart better answers the question ‘what share of each category’s laureates are women’?






Before you make a chart, ask…




What is my question, or the story I want to tell?
Which of the things in the cards above am I trying to show?
What type of data are the variables involved?
Which chart type, and which aesthetics, fit both?

If you can’t answer the first question, no chart type will help!

title: 29  More chart types
text:
Check your understanding
1. A student wants to show how the number of pages in published novels is spread out: are most novels about the same length, or are there lots of very short and very long ones? Which chart types would be suitable, and which geoms would they use?






Answer





This is a question about a distribution of a continuous variable. A histogram (geom_histogram()) or density plot (geom_density()) would show the shape of the distribution. A boxplot (geom_boxplot()) would also work, and would be particularly useful for comparing the distribution between groups, for example novels from different decades.



2. A chart shows the number of books published each year from 1800 to 1900, for eight different countries, as eight coloured lines on one chart. The lines overlap and are hard to tell apart. What one line of code could you add to make it clearer, and what else would you change?






Answer





Add facet_wrap(~ country) to make small multiples: one small line chart per country. You could then remove color = country from the aes(), because each panel is already labelled with its country, so the colour and the legend are no longer needed.

title: 32  More Data Visualisation
text:
Last week we covered the basics of ggplot2: mapping data to aesthetics, drawing it with a geometry, and the main chart types you’ll use most often (bars, points, lines, histograms, and boxplots).
This week builds on that in two directions.
First, we’ll look at gestalt principles and pre-attentive attributes - two frameworks from psychology which help explain why data visualisation works as a way of communicating information, and which give us some vocabulary for talking critically about our own and others’ charts (useful for the in-class critique exercise at the end of that page).
Second, we’ll go a layer deeper into ggplot2 itself, and look at scales. Scales control how the values in your data get mapped onto a chart - where a point sits on the x axis, which colour a bar is filled with, how big a symbol is drawn. Choosing sensible scales (or occasionally choosing misleading ones) has a big effect on what a viewer takes away from a chart, so it’s worth understanding how to control them deliberately rather than always accepting ggplot’s defaults.
Over the rest of this part, we’ll cover:

Position scales: setting axis limits, breaks, and labels, and reordering categories on a chart.
Date scales: the same idea, applied to dates - very common in humanities data.
Colour and size scales: choosing sequential, diverging, and categorical palettes, including ones which are safe for colour vision deficiency.

title: 33  Gestalt Principles
text:
Gestalt Principles
Gestalt principles were developed from the late 1800s and could be considered part of the discipline of psychology and philosophy. Gestalt principles are related to perception: the basic theory is that we perceive visual forms as a whole, rather than each part separately.
In other words, we simplify our visual stimuli in order to make sense of what we are seeing, and the wider world.
The developers of Gestalt boiled this down to a series of principles, which they say govern how we do this simplification. The data visualisation types and default settings we use naturally use these principles - we don’t need to actively think about them most of the time. However, it’s worth understanding them to have some kind of theory as to why data visualisation works.
The principles which apply particularly to data visualisation are:

title: 33  Gestalt Principles
text:
Proximity
Similarity
Enclosure
Closure
Continuity
Connection



Proximity
When objects are placed close together, our mind intuitively infers a connection between them.
Take this scatterplot, which visualises the relationship between bill length and flipper size in a dataset of penguin observations.
Something we might notice is that there are roughly three clusters of points which are closer together than they are to the other clusters. We intuitively realise that there is some significance to these points being placed close together (in this case, each cluster represents a different species of penguin).









In more general terms of design, it can also be useful to think about proximity - different elements of charts should be close together, such as labels and legend.


Similarity
This principle states that objects which are a similar (or the same) size, shape or colour will be perceived as part of the same group. This is a very useful way to draw attention to significant groups in our data. If we add colour to the previous example, the distinctiveness of the species is even clearer:











Enclosure
This principle says that objects within the same border will be perceived as a group. Again, this can be exploited in data visualisation to highlight groups within our data.









We’ll learn how to add these kinds of things in a future class.


Closure
Closure is the principle that we tend to ‘close’ unfinished objects to make them whole. This is perhaps not used as much as some of the others in data visualisation, but, for instance, we can think of the way in which we perceive dashed lines as a solid line:











Continuity









This principle states that we naturally try to organise objects when they are placed one after another. The obvious use of this is in graphs showing change over time. When drawn as lines, we make the natural assumption that the objects (in this case, position on a graph) are in a sequence and are related to each other.


Connection
This principle states that if objects are connected, we perceive them as a unified entity. This is clearly demonstrated in the chart below: the connection between the first and second points helps to guide us to consider the values together and make comparisons between them.

title: 33  Gestalt Principles
text:
Pre-attentive attributes
The second framework mentioned at the start of this chapter is pre-attentive attributes. These are visual properties that our brains process automatically and almost instantly (in well under half a second), before we consciously focus our attention on them - long before we could read a label or count individual items.
Attributes such as colour, size, orientation, and motion are all processed pre-attentively. This is why a single red point among a field of grey ones seems to ‘pop out’ immediately, without you needing to scan the image - our visual system detects this kind of difference automatically.
This is directly useful for data visualisation: if you want a viewer to notice something at a glance, map it to a pre-attentive attribute (like colour or size), rather than relying on something that requires careful, conscious reading (like a small text label).

title: 34  Chart scales
text:
Scales
The process by which this happens involves scales. Scales are the next ‘layer’ in our ggplot object. Scales control the mapping from data to aesthetics. Data visualisations cannot work without scales, so ggplot2 will automatically add them to your plots, but knowing how to control these and the various options they have available will allow you to have much more control over the look of your visualisations.
We won’t go into the theory of how ggplot2 works with scales in too much detail, but concentrate on some practical code, examples and tips which I think have the most impact on controlling the aspects of your plots you would expect to be able to do.

title: 34  Chart scales
text:
Note



These scales are communicated to the viewer by means of an axis or a legend, which we’ll cover afterwards.

title: 34  Chart scales
text:
Why scales matter
It’s worth pausing on why this is worth learning properly, rather than just accepting ggplot’s defaults. The same data, drawn with different scale choices, can tell quite different stories - not because the numbers have changed, but because of where the axis starts, or which colours suggest which categories are related.
Take this chart of the number of Nobel laureates awarded per decade. On the left, the y axis runs from 0; on the right, it’s limited to close to the actual range of the data:


Code
library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)

laureates_df <- read_csv('laureates_df.csv', show_col_types = FALSE)
prize_df <- read_csv('prize_df.csv', show_col_types = FALSE)

nobel_by_decade <- laureates_df |>
  left_join(prize_df, by = 'prize_id') |>
  filter(award_year < 2020) |>
  mutate(decade = floor(award_year / 10) * 10) |>
  count(decade)

p1 <- nobel_by_decade |>
  ggplot(aes(x = decade, y = n)) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 125)) +
  labs(title = "Starting at 0", y = "Laureates per decade") +
  theme_bw()

p2 <- nobel_by_decade |>
  ggplot(aes(x = decade, y = n)) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(35, 120)) +
  labs(title = "Zoomed in", y = "Laureates per decade") +
  theme_bw()

p1 + p2









Both charts are technically accurate - nothing has been faked. But the one on the right makes the growth (and the dips around the two World Wars) look far more dramatic, simply by choosing different limits. Neither version is automatically ‘the’ correct one to use (sometimes zooming in is exactly the right choice, if the small changes are genuinely the point), but you should always make that choice deliberately, and be able to justify it, rather than leaving it to chance or - worse - picking whichever version tells the story you wanted to tell.
The same logic applies to colour, size, and the other scales we’ll cover in this part: they’re not just decoration, they’re doing real interpretive work.

title: 34  Chart scales
text:
Aesthetics
Recall from earlier this week that we learned about different aesthetics: position, colour, size, shape, linetype, linewidth, and transparency. This chapter on scales will mostly cover position and colour, and to a lesser extent, size. The scales for the other aesthetics are less interesting (you’re less likely to want to change the defaults), so we won’t look at these. But be aware they also have scales which can be overwritten or adjusted.

title: 35  Position scales
text:
Position scales
Scales are added to ggplot2 plots in much the same way as other layers. First a +, followed by the name of the scale. Options are specified within the parentheses of the scale name.
Scales are either continuous or discrete, depending on the data. A bar chart generally contains one continuous variable (a count) and one discrete variable (the different categories, generally one for each bar), whereas a line chart generally has two continuous variables.
The most common position scales are scale_x_continuous and scale_y_continuous, which simply map linearly from a data value to a location on the plot. If you plot continuous data on an axis, ggplot will automatically add these to your plot. You only need to specify them explicitly if you want to change any of the default options.
In this chart, which we have seen before, ggplot has automatically created continuous scales to represent the award_year and n (the number of laureates that year). Each point is placed in a position based on these scales. These are represented on the chart as the x and y axis, so we know what each position refers to.
There are two useful things we can change with the default continuous scale: limits and breaks.
To make changes to the default scale, we add scale_x_continuous or scale_y_continuous following a + sign to the plot.

title: 35  Position scales
text:
Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.


Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.


Limits specify the limits of the scale - the start and end points of the x and y axes.
Breaks specify which points and ticks should be drawn on the x and y axes.



Limits
To change the limits, add limits = followed by the start and end point of the limit you want, within a vector using c(), as in the example below:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
You can see that it has limited the years to 1980 at earliest and 2000 at the latest.
You’ll also see a warning: “Removed 100 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range”. This tells you something important about how limits work. They don’t just hide the data outside the limits: they remove it, before anything is drawn. Here the data has one row per year from 1901 to 2024, and only the 21 rows from 1980 to 2000 are left.
For a line chart like this one, that makes no difference to what you see. But it does matter for any geom that calculates something from the data before drawing it, such as a histogram (which counts the values in each bin) or a boxplot (which calculates the median and quartiles). If you set limits on one of these, the calculation only uses the values that are left, so the chart can change, and not just zoom in. Whenever you see this warning, check how many rows were removed, and ask yourself whether that matters.
Try it yourself: set the limits of the y axis to 0 and 20

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.


Breaks
Breaks control which axis ticks, lines and labels are shown. Ggplot picks defaults according to the data but you can override them.
Change the breaks by adding breaks = to the plot, followed by a vector (a list) of the values you want to specify.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Try it yourself: Set the breaks for the y axis to every 2 instead of every 5

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.






Tip



It would quickly get tedious if you wanted to specify a large number of axis ticks. R has a function called seq(), which allows you to create a sequence of numbers according to simple rules. seq() needs a from, to and by argument. For example we could specify that the plot show values every two years by adding the following:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.



Minor breaks
Note that changing the breaks also changes the vertical lines in the plot. By default, ggplot draws a line for each break, as well as a fainter line in between each break, called minor breaks. You can override the positions for these minor breaks, too.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
You can also add different labels for your axis, using the ‘labels’ argument:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Try it yourself: copy the chart above, but change the minor breaks to every 5 years, and the labels for the major breaks to ‘First Year’, ‘Second Year’, and so forth.



Scales with bar charts
Bar charts using geom_col generally have a discrete scale instead of a continuous scale on the x axis. Each bar represents a category rather than a numeric value. The name of this is scale_x_discrete, which is added automatically by ggplot.






Note



A bar chart can also have a numeric variable on the x axis, for example if we made the plot above, but with geom_col instead of geom_line. In this case, though it will contain individual discrete bars for each year, ggplot2 will still give it a continuous scale.


By default, this will be ordered alphabetically. Reordering these is a very common data visualisation task. Take the following example, which counts the number of laureates in each prize category:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
In many cases we would want to reorder the categories by the value on the y axis - so that the highest appear at the top. We can do this not within the scale but by using reorder in the code of the plot itself:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

title: 35  Position scales
text:
Coord_flip()
A final useful function is coord_flip. This flips the coordinates of a plot, and reverses the position of the x and y axes.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.






Note



Note that we have removed the desc() so that the highest value is at the top rather than the bottom.


This is particularly useful for a chart with lots of values, because the labels are much easier to read when they are placed along the y-axis - especially if it is going to be viewed online. It’s also handy here for another reason: some of these category names (“Physiology or Medicine”, “Economic Sciences”) are quite long, and read much more comfortably running horizontally than squeezed onto a vertical x axis.

title: 37  Data challenge 3 (alternative): How has music changed over time?
text:
The data
In 2019 the data scientist Kaylin Pavlik wanted to know whether a computer could tell musical genres apart just from how songs sound. She searched Spotify for playlists in six genres (EDM, Latin, pop, R&B, rap and rock, each split into four subgenres), and downloaded every song on 471 of them. For each song, Spotify’s API gave her its release date, its popularity, and a set of audio features: numbers that Spotify’s own algorithms calculate from the recording. The dataset was shared through TidyTuesday in January 2020.
There is one row per song on a playlist. The columns you’ll use most are:
crumbs: 37  Data challenge 3 (alternative): How has music changed over time?

title: 37  Data challenge 3 (alternative): How has music changed over time?
text:
track_name, track_artist, track_id: the song, who it’s by, and Spotify’s ID for it.
playlist_genre and playlist_subgenre: the genre of the playlist the song was found on.
track_album_release_date: when the album the song is on came out.
track_popularity: Spotify’s popularity score in 2020, from 0 to 100.
duration_ms: the length of the song, in milliseconds.
danceability, energy and valence: scores from 0 to 1. Valence is how positive (happy, cheerful) a song sounds: a high score is happy, a low score sad or angry.
loudness: the average loudness, in decibels. The values are negative: the closer to 0, the louder.
tempo: the speed, in beats per minute.
crumbs: 37  Data challenge 3 (alternative): How has music changed over time?

title: 37  Data challenge 3 (alternative): How has music changed over time?
text:
Setting up
You don’t need to download anything: read_csv() can read a file straight from a web address. Copy this code into the first chunk of your .Rmd and run it. It adds two columns: year (the first four characters of the release date, as a number) and duration_min (the length in minutes).
library(tidyverse)

spotify <- read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2020/2020-01-21/spotify_songs.csv")

spotify <- spotify |>
  mutate(year = as.numeric(str_sub(track_album_release_date, 1, 4)),
         duration_min = duration_ms / 60000)
spotify should have 32,833 rows. If your internet is slow, save a copy in your project folder with write_csv(spotify, "spotify_songs.csv"), and read that next time.
Most release dates are written in full (2019-06-14), but some are just a year (2012). Why does str_sub() work for both? (1,855 dates are just a year)

title: 37  Data challenge 3 (alternative): How has music changed over time?

Part 1: genres and artists

Count the rows by playlist_genre, and make a bar chart of the result. Use reorder() to put the bars in order of size. (edm: 6,043)
Count the rows by playlist_genre and playlist_subgenre (put both inside count()). How many subgenres are there? (24) Make a bar chart with the subgenres on the x axis, flipped with coord_flip() and ordered with reorder(). Then map fill to playlist_genre. Which is the biggest subgenre? (progressive electro house: 1,809)
The subgenres of each genre are scattered across the chart, but you can still pick them out. Which Gestalt principle lets you do that?
Who are the artists with the most songs in the dataset? Count the rows by track_artist, keep the top 15 with slice_max(n, n = 15), and save the result as top_artists. Make an ordered, flipped bar chart. (Martin Garrix: 161)
Is each artist tied to one genre? Filter spotify to the artists in top_artists (use %in% with top_artists$track_artist), then count by track_artist and playlist_genre. Make a flipped bar chart with fill = playlist_genre, then add position = 'fill' to geom_col(). Which three artists are almost entirely in one genre, and which artist is spread most evenly? (Queen: 134 of 136 songs are rock; Drake’s biggest genre has only 36 of his 100 songs)

title: 37  Data challenge 3 (alternative): How has music changed over time?
text:
Part 2: songs over time

A song can be on more than one playlist. How many different songs are there? Use n_distinct() on track_id. (28,356) Which song appears most often? Count by track_id, track_name and track_artist, and sort the result. In how many genres does it appear? (10 rows, in five genres)
When we count songs over time, a song that appears on ten playlists would be counted ten times. So we’ll keep just one row per song. Run this code:

songs <- spotify |>
  distinct(track_id, .keep_all = TRUE)
distinct() keeps one row for each track_id, and .keep_all = TRUE keeps all the other columns too. songs should have 28,356 rows. Each song now has only the genre of the first playlist it was found on. Use songs from now on.

Count songs by year, and draw it as a bar chart. Which year has the most songs? (2019: 7,406) How many songs came out in 2010 or later? (20,460, almost three-quarters) What are the oldest songs in the dataset? (two, from 1957)
Why do you think so few old songs are in the dataset? Think about how it was made: who makes playlists, and when were these playlists collected?
Did the genres change over time? Add a decade column to songs with mutate(decade = floor(year / 10) * 10), and keep only the decades from 1970 to 2010. Save the result as decades. (27,595 rows) Count decades by decade and playlist_genre, and make a bar chart with fill = playlist_genre and position = 'fill'. Use scale_x_continuous() to put a break at each decade. (rock: 89% of songs from the 1970s, 7% from the 2010s)
Keep that chart in mind. If we compare songs from the 1970s with songs from the 2010s, what are we really comparing?

title: 37  Data challenge 3 (alternative): How has music changed over time?
section: Part 3: what does each genre sound like?
text:
Part 3: what does each genre sound like?

Draw a histogram of duration_min from songs, with binwidth = 0.25. What is the median length of a song? (3.6 minutes) Find the shortest and longest songs with slice_min() and slice_max(). (4 seconds; 8.6 minutes)
Which genre is the most danceable? Make a boxplot with playlist_genre on the x axis and danceability on the y axis. Put the boxes in order with reorder(playlist_genre, danceability): this orders them by the average danceability of each genre. Then calculate the median for each genre with group_by() and summarise(). (rap: 0.734; rock: 0.522)
Are loud songs energetic? Make a scatterplot with loudness on the x axis and energy on the y axis. With 28,000 points it’s just a blob, so set alpha = 0.1. Should alpha go inside or outside aes()? Describe the relationship in one sentence.
Add facet_wrap(~ playlist_genre) to the scatterplot. Which genre’s points sit furthest to the top right? Check your answer with the median energy of each genre. (edm: 0.838)

title: 37  Data challenge 3 (alternative): How has music changed over time?
text:
Part 4: are songs getting shorter?
Music journalists often say that songs are getting shorter, because streaming services pay per play, and listeners skip. Does this dataset agree?

Filter songs to the years 1970 to 2019 (2020 had only just started when the data was collected). Then use group_by(year) and summarise() to make two columns: songs = n() and median_duration = median(duration_min). Save the result as durations.
Draw median_duration as a line chart with points on top. Use scale_x_continuous() to put a break every five years. In which year were songs longest, and how long were they in 2019? (1990: 4.6 minutes; 2019: 3.2)
Now add scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 5)). How does the drop look now? Which version of the chart would you use, and why?
Remember Part 2: the old songs are mostly rock, and the new ones aren’t. Maybe songs are only getting shorter because rock songs are long? Use decades to calculate the median duration (and the number of songs, with n()) for each decade and playlist_genre. Draw a line chart with decade on the x axis and colour = playlist_genre. Are songs from the 2010s shorter than songs from the 1990s in every genre? Which genre changed most? (yes; rap went from 4.4 to 3.3 minutes)
One point on that chart is much higher than the rest. Look at its number of songs. Should we trust it? (edm in the 1970s: 7.6 minutes, from 4 songs)
Harder: has the sound of music changed too? Starting from songs filtered to 1970–2019, use group_by(year) and summarise() to calculate the median loudness, valence and danceability for each year. Use pivot_longer() to put the three medians in one column, and draw a line chart with facet_wrap(), one panel per feature. Try scales = "free_y": why do you need it here? In which year were songs loudest, and when were they least happy? (loudest: 2013; lowest valence: 2014) Look up the “loudness war”.

Write a short paragraph (four or five sentences) about popular music, based on your charts. Pick the chart you think tells the most interesting story, and say what it shows. Then think about the data. These songs come from playlists one person found on Spotify in late 2019, in six genres she chose. The audio features come from Spotify’s own algorithms, which aren’t public (and which Spotify stopped sharing with new apps in 2024). The year is when the album came out, not the song. How might each of these things affect what your chart shows?

title: 39  Colour and size scales
text:
Colour scales with continuous and discrete data
Remember the data types from last week? How colour is mapped to data, and which scales we can and should choose, is highly dependent on the data type given. Remember too that colour is found either in the colour aesthetic (for example for geom_point) but also in the fill aesthetic (such as the fill colour of a bar chart). Both work in the same way, but use a slightly different scale name.
Mapping categorical data will result in a discrete scale, by default scale_colour_discrete or scale_fill_discrete. With this scale, ggplot will choose colours with the aim of making them as distinct from each other as possible.
Mapping numerical data will result in a continuous scale, by default scale_colour_continuous or scale_fill_continuous. With this scale, ggplot will choose a colour range where one end of the hue or saturation will be mapped to high values and the other end to low values.
Let’s see how this works by mapping the fill in a bar chart to numerical and categorical data variables. To demonstrate we’ll take the Nobel Prize dataset from last week and summarise it by category, as before:
The pct_female variable is numerical, so if we set it to the fill aesthetic, ggplot2 will pick a continuous scale. The default scale maps high values as light blue and low values as dark blue.
The category variable is itself categorical, so if we also map it to the fill aesthetic, ggplot2 will pick a discrete scale. By default, ggplot spaces the colours as evenly as possible around the colour wheel, so that each category gets as distinct a colour as possible - though as the number of categories grows, the colours inevitably become harder to tell apart, so it’s worth choosing a more deliberate palette (see below) once you have more than a handful of categories.
Note that in order to communicate how values have been mapped to colours, ggplot automatically includes a legend, which looks different depending on the type of scale used.
There are lots of ways to choose different colour scales. In all these cases, the word colour is interchangeable with the word fill within the names of the scales.

title: Data sources for assignments
text:
Importing a dataset and dataset standards
For these assignments, you’ll need to begin by importing your dataset as an object into the RStudio environment. How you do this depends a little on the standard of your dataset. As we’re working with tabular data on this course, your data should in most cases be in one of these formats:
You can read data originating from either your local machine, or directly from the internet in some cases.
Whatever dataset you use, a really important task is to read the documentation available, so you understand, as best as possible, how it was made and who was responsible for it. If you can’t find out where a dataset came from, don’t use it.

title: Data sources for assignments
text:
Comma separated values (files ending in .csv). A very common tabular data format. Use read_csv() from the Tidyverse package readr (remember to load the package first) to read the file in to R.
Tab separated values (files ending in .tsv). Another common tabular format. Use read_tsv() from the Tidyverse package readr to read the file.
Excel files: Microsoft proprietary format, which can contain multiple sheets. Use read_excel() from the Tidyverse package readxl to read the file.
Google sheets. You can read Google sheets directly from the internet using the package googlesheets4.



If you’re loading from your local machine, save the file in your project folder first.
If you know the path online to a file in one of the formats above, you can simply add the full path as the filename within quotation marks, e.g. read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/yann-ryan/infovis_data/main/nobel/laureates_df.csv'). For files on GitHub, make sure you use the raw version of the file (click the ‘Raw’ button on the file’s page and copy that address) - the normal GitHub page is a web page, not a csv file.








Warning



Some datasets are too big to work with comfortably on a laptop: R has to load the whole file into your computer’s memory, which can make everything very slow, or stop with an error. Datasets below which are likely to be this big are marked (large). If you use one, filter it down to the part you need as early as possible, and save that smaller version to work with.

title: Data sources for assignments
text:
Datasets used on the course
The datasets we’ve worked with in class are relatively clean and simple, by humanities data standards. For Assignment 1 especially, I highly recommend using one of these: data cleaning and figuring out formats can be very time consuming, so unless you are very comfortable with these things, think carefully before choosing a bespoke dataset.

The Titanic dataset. There are many versions of this on the internet, because it is widely used in machine learning problems. I created a version based on this dataset, because it contains the full list and hasn’t been divided into different parts for training and testing machine learning algorithms. There is a little information on how the dataset was constructed, but unfortunately the link to further information is no longer working. My version is available here.
The Bellevue Almshouse data. Records of immigrants who were admitted to the Bellevue Almshouse (house for the poor) in New York in the 1840s. You can find more information and links to the data here.
The Movie Dialogue dataset. You can find more information about this dataset here. I created the third file, imdb_genre, from a larger IMDB dataset. You can find that file here.
The Nobel Prize Winners dataset. Two tables, with information on the Nobel Prizes and the Nobel Prize winners. I created this using the official Nobel API. You can find the files here.

title: Data sources for assignments
text:
Suggested datasets
If you’d like to try something different, the datasets below are similar in spirit to the ones we’ve used in class: tabular, reasonably clean, documented, and about culture or history. Each comes with an idea of the kind of question you could ask of it, but these are just starting points.
When choosing, keep to something broadly humanities-related (so not primarily natural sciences or economics), and check before you commit that there is documentation telling you where the data came from and how it was made - you’ll need it to write a good report.

Good for a first visualisation (Assignment 1)

Art history textbooks (TidyTuesday). Every artist who appears in the two most widely used art history survey textbooks (Janson’s and Gardner’s) across all their editions, with the artists’ gender, ethnicity, nationality, and how much page space each one received. A very direct way into questions about the canon: who gets included, and how has that changed over time? Comes from the R package arthistory.
Eurovision (TidyTuesday). Results of every Eurovision Song Contest, plus the votes cast between countries. Good for rankings over time, and the voting table invites questions about ‘bloc voting’ and which countries favour which (there’s even a mapping project hiding in there).
Bob Ross paintings (TidyTuesday). Every painting from the TV show The Joy of Painting, with the colours used in each one, by season and episode. Small, friendly, and nice for experimenting with colour scales - you can use the actual hex codes of the paints.
Billboard Hot 100 (TidyTuesday). Weekly positions of every song on the US Billboard chart since 1958, joined to Spotify’s audio features (danceability, tempo, and so on). Has songs got shorter, sadder, or faster? A good chance to practise dates and joins.
The Tate collection. Metadata for around 70,000 artworks and 3,500 artists in the Tate’s collection: titles, dates, media, dimensions, acquisition year, and artists’ birth and death places. It’s a 2014 snapshot and no longer updated (which is worth mentioning in your report!), but it is clean and well structured.
The Museum of Modern Art collection. Similar to the Tate data but bigger and regularly updated: artworks with dates, departments, dimensions and acquisition dates, plus artists’ nationality, gender and birth/death years. FiveThirtyEight’s guide to MoMA’s paintings gives a sense of what’s possible.
Post45 Data Collective. Peer-reviewed datasets about twentieth- and twenty-first-century literature, each with a short essay explaining how it was made. Good choices are the New York Times hardcover fiction bestsellers (1931-2020), the index of major literary prizes in the US, and the British literary prizes dataset. Questions about gender, genre and prestige come out of these very naturally.
Project Gutenberg metadata, via the R package gutenbergr. Metadata (not text) for the tens of thousands of books on Project Gutenberg: title, author, authors’ birth and death years, language and subject headings, loaded with gutenberg_metadata, gutenberg_authors and gutenberg_subjects. What does the ‘public domain canon’ look like?



Good for a map (Assignment 2)

Shakespeare and Company Project. Records from Sylvia Beach’s lending library in interwar Paris, with geocoded addresses for its members. An article describes the data, which is divided into members, books, and events (mostly library loans). Map where readers lived, or join the tables to see who borrowed what.
Rijksmonumentenregister. The Dutch register of national monuments - around 60,000 protected buildings and sites, with their type, building period and location. A good local option: map monuments by type or era in Leiden or your home town. Bulk downloads are available via data.overheid.nl (search for ‘rijksmonumenten’).
Dutch-Asiatic Shipping (Huygens Institute). Around 8,000 voyages made by VOC ships between the Netherlands and Asia, 1595-1795, with ships, dates, ports of departure and arrival, and crew numbers. Good for maps of routes and for time series.
Pantheon. Tens of thousands of ‘famous’ historical people, with birthplaces (including coordinates), occupations and a measure of how much their Wikipedia pages are viewed. Fun to map, but also an excellent dataset to be critical about: what does ‘famous’ mean, and whose fame does Wikipedia record?
A cross-verified database of notable people (Laouenan et al., 2022) (large). Around 2.3 million notable people from 3500 BC to 2018, assembled from Wikipedia and Wikidata, with birth and death dates and places, gender and occupation. Much bigger and more systematic than Pantheon; filter it down to a period or region that interests you.
Pleiades. A gazetteer of tens of thousands of places in the ancient world, with coordinates, place types and the periods in which they were in use. Download the CSV ‘dumps’. Good for anyone interested in classics or archaeology.
Mapping Inequality. Digitised versions of the 1930s US government ‘redlining’ maps, which graded neighbourhoods by supposed mortgage risk, largely along racial lines. Downloadable as GeoJSON, so you can practise with polygons rather than points.
The World Atlas of Language Structures, based on WALS. Linguistic features of the world’s languages, with coordinates. It’s a little difficult to find what you need, but the languages table is the most important. Pair it with this dataset of endangered and extinct languages.



More ambitious
These are bigger, messier, or need more care, but reward the effort if you’re feeling confident.

SlaveVoyages. The Trans-Atlantic and Intra-American slave trade databases: records of around 36,000 voyages, with ports, dates, and numbers of enslaved people embarked and disembarked. One of the most important datasets in digital history, and one which demands careful thought about how to visualise human suffering.
The Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access (large). Around half a million objects from the Met’s collection in one CSV, covering everything from ancient Egypt to modern design. Lots of missing values and inconsistencies, which is realistic and makes for good discussion in a report.
Old Bailey Online and the Digital Panopticon. Nearly 200,000 criminal trials at London’s central criminal court, 1674-1913, and the later lives of convicts. Getting tabular data out takes some work; Sharon Howard’s blog posts show how, with R and tidyverse code.
British Library newspapers title list. Every newspaper title held by the British Library, with places and dates of publication. Good for mapping the growth of the press.
litRiddle. Data from a large Dutch reader survey about contemporary novels, combined with information about the books and authors. There’s also an R package: install.packages("litRiddle").
IMDb non-commercial datasets (large). Every film and TV title on IMDb, with genres, runtimes, ratings and cast and crew.
HathiTrust Hathifiles (large). Catalogue metadata (not content) for the millions of volumes digitised by HathiTrust. Look for the most recent file starting with hathi_full.

title: Data sources for assignments
text:
Data repositories and lists
There are many, many sources of datasets available online. Look for relatively simple csv and tsv files or sets of files, and avoid those that mention APIs or Linked Open Data unless you are comfortable working with these things.

National and international statistics

CBS Statline: Dutch statistics. Also an R package, cbsodataR.
Eurostat: official EU statistics, at different regional levels - including cultural statistics such as cultural employment and participation.
e-Stat: official statistics repository of Japan. The statistics dashboard is particularly useful.



Humanities repositories

Journal of Open Humanities Data. Short articles describing humanities datasets, with the data attached and possible use cases. A great place to find well-documented data.
Post45 Data Collective (see above).
TidyTuesday. A weekly data challenge with a large archive of datasets, organised by year and week. Many aren’t relevant to the humanities, but those that are tend to be clean and documented.
DANS Social Sciences and Humanities: the Dutch national repository. Lots of datasets, but they can be very specific and not always easy to use.
KB Labs datasets from the Dutch national library (many are text-based but some are structured).
The Pudding has some nice and often fun datasets, though they have a very American focus.
Melanie Walsh’s Introduction to Cultural Analytics has a page of datasets. Not all are tabular - some are primarily text, which is outside the scope of this course.
The Google dataset search. However, make sure you can trace back the provenance!
The ‘DH toychest’ datasets and this list of museum APIs. Both are old, so expect some broken links, but there are still useful things there.







Tip



For very large datasets, it may also be helpful to use an R package such as data.table which is more efficient than Tidyverse for working with very large data. data.table has a very different syntax to the Tidyverse, but there is a package, tidytable, which converts between the two.

title: Data sources for assignments
text:
R packages
There are many R ‘dataset packages’. These can be very useful, because accessing the data is simple - you just need to install a package and then follow some instructions to load the dataset, rather than find and upload a spreadsheet file. They are also generally formatted so they are easy to use in R.

HistData: classic datasets from the history of data visualisation - including Florence Nightingale’s data on causes of death in the Crimean War, John Snow’s cholera map, and Minard’s data on Napoleon’s march on Moscow. You could recreate (and improve on?) a famous chart.
arthistory: the art history textbook data described above.
gutenbergr: Project Gutenberg metadata (see above).
taylor: the complete discography of Taylor Swift, with Spotify audio features and lyrics. See the package website.
refugees: UNHCR data on refugees and displaced people, from 1951 onwards.
A huge list of datasets in R packages here - but again, try to only use those with good documentation.


R packages which connect to an API

The osmdata package. Download geographic data from OpenStreetMap through R. Very fun to work with, though takes some understanding of the queries. Try a tutorial here if you’re interested.
spotifyr allows you to download data from Spotify. You need to register for an API key. Be aware that since late 2024 Spotify no longer gives new apps access to its ‘audio features’ (danceability, energy and so on), so much of what you’ll see in older tutorials won’t work. Datasets which already include these features, such as the Billboard data above, are a better bet.

title: Data sources for assignments
text:
Social media data
Unfortunately, doing analysis on social media data has become very difficult in the last few years as companies have locked down their services. Twitter/X ended free and academic access to its API in 2023, which means older collections of tweet IDs can no longer be ‘hydrated’ into actual tweets, and Reddit has also heavily restricted access. Unless you have a ready-made, documented dataset (and permission to use it), I’d avoid social media data for this course.

title: Data sources for assignments
text:
Inspiration for your reports

Current Research in Digital History (short historical essays with graphics).
Journal of Digital History (digital history articles with a code layer).
Journal of Cultural Analytics (computational articles on culture, often with visual elements).
The Pudding (data journalism visual essays with interactive elements).
Visualizing Emancipation (a nice example of a visual essay aimed at an academic readership).
The Killing Times (example of an interactive visual essay, for those interested in using Shiny).
Short visual essays by FiveThirtyEight such as this one, and their guide to MoMA’s paintings, which is a nice example of the kind of project you could make with collections data.
Sharon Howard’s data blogs. Some use other tech, but many are straightforward R/tidyverse visualisations with historical data, such as here.
The Programming Historian (peer-reviewed tutorials, several of which use R and historical data).
Cool stuff made with cultural heritage APIs.

title: Critique gallery
text:
1 Diagram of the causes of mortality in the army in the East
Florence Nightingale, 1858
Deaths of British soldiers in the Crimean War, month by month, divided by cause. Nightingale used it to argue for better sanitation in army hospitals.
Open full size



2 Napoleon’s Russian campaign of 1812
Charles Joseph Minard, 1869
The size of Napoleon’s army as it marched to Moscow and retreated, with the temperature on the way back. Often called one of the best charts ever made: is it?
Open full size



3 Assessed value of household and kitchen furniture owned by Georgia Negroes
W.E.B. Du Bois and students at Atlanta University, 1900
One of a series of hand-drawn charts made for the 1900 Paris Exposition, showing the progress of Black Americans since the end of slavery.
Open full size



4 Deaths from cholera in Soho, London, 1854
John Snow, published 1855
Each death in the cholera outbreak of 1854, drawn at the house where it happened, with the public water pumps. Snow used it to argue that cholera spread through drinking water, not bad air.
Open full size

title: Critique gallery
text:
Round 1: data and aesthetics
Thu 12 Nov, together with round 2. Uses Data Visualisation Basics and More chart types.

What is one observation in this visualisation: a person, a month, a year, a country? What are the variables?
What type is each variable: categorical, ordinal, discrete, or continuous?
Which aesthetic is each variable mapped to (position, size, colour, shape, …)? Is anything mapped to more than one aesthetic?
What kind of chart is it? Using the cards in Choosing a chart, what is it trying to show: amounts, a ranking, a distribution, a relationship, change over time, part-to-whole, a comparison, or something spatial?
Are the scales used consistently? Could you read off an actual value if you wanted to?
What is the main message, in one sentence? Is the chart effective at getting it across?

title: Critique gallery
text:
Round 2: perception and design
Thu 12 Nov, with Gestalt Principles.

Where does your eye go first? Is that the most important thing?
Think about the ‘user journey’ through the visualisation. Is it obvious what you’re meant to look at, and in what order? How long did it take you to understand how to read it?
Which Gestalt principles are being used (proximity, similarity, connection, closure, enclosure, continuity)? How do they help, or get in the way?
Does the design group together things that shouldn’t be grouped, or split up things that belong together?
What would you remove, and what would you add, to make it easier to read?

title: Critique gallery
text:
Round 3: accessibility and ethics
Tue 24 Nov, with Ethics and data visualisation and Data Visualisation and Accessibility.
Accessibility:

Using what the accessibility chapter says about colour vision deficiency, which colours on your sheet would be hard to tell apart for someone with red-green colour blindness? Does the meaning depend on colour alone, or is there another way to tell things apart (position, labels, shape)?
Is there enough contrast? Is the text big enough to read?
How would the visualisation work for someone with low vision, or who uses a screen reader? As a group, write a one- or two-sentence alt text for it.

Ethics:

Who made it, when, for whom, and why? Is it trying to persuade? Is that purpose open, or hidden behind an appearance of neutrality?
Where does the data come from, and how was it collected? Who or what is counted, and who or what is missing? Is the creator open about this?
What role does emotion play? Does the design make you feel something about the data?
What do you imagine is the positionality of the person or people who made it? What is yours, and how does it affect how you read it?
Pick one item from the ethics checklist (for example, ‘show uncertainty’ or ‘make the invisible visible’). How well does the visualisation do on it?

title: Critique gallery
section: Round 4: maps as arguments, and a verdict
text:
Round 4: maps as arguments, and a verdict
Thu 26 Nov, with Maps as data visualisation.

How does location matter in your visualisation? If it’s a map: what does each area or point stand for, and what has been left off? If it isn’t: would a map show something it misses, or would it hide something it shows? (Minard’s chart is a bit of both!)
For the map (4): what does each mark stand for, and what else has Snow chosen to draw, or leave off? How does the map make an argument, and what would a reader in 1855 have needed to believe it? For the others: does Minard’s or Nightingale’s use of space work like a map, even though only one of them is?
Look back at your notes from the other three rounds. As a group, write a short critique of the visualisation, in four sentences:

what it shows, and for whom
one thing it does well, and why
one weakness, and why
one concrete change you would make, and how you would do it with ggplot2 (name the geom, scale, or other function)


This last step is exactly what the exam critique question asks you to do.
